To happen, to occur, to arrive: this is the event that occurs, the action that is realized. In Ecclesiastes 11:3, if the clouds fill up, that is what "happens", what occurs naturally. 4. To have as a result, to lead to: this is the effect, the consequence, the outcome. In Ecclesiastes 2:22, the text asks what "effect" comes to man from his work, meaning what profit or usefulness results from it.
H1933B.origine: The Hebrew verb הָוָה (havah) is one of the oldest forms of the verb "to be" in Hebrew. It belongs to the same family as הִוָּה (hivvah, "he showed") and shares a root with the noun הַוָּה (hawwah, "the ruin"). This verb expresses the passage to the state of being, unlike the verb קוּם (qum, "to rise") which emphasizes action or the verb יֵשׁ (yesh, "he exists") which simply affirms presence. The Aramaic equivalent is הֲוָא (hava), used in the Aramaic passages of Daniel and Ezra.
H1933B.emploi: The verb havah appears about 5 times in the biblical usages preserved here, mainly in historical and wisdom texts. It is used to express a change of state (to become king, to become rebellious), an occurrence (what happens, occurs) or a consequence (the effect, the profit). The meaning varies according to the context: sometimes it emphasizes the transformation of a person or a people, sometimes it simply designates what happens or ensues. It is found in both the narratives of Nehemiah and the wisdom of Ecclesiastes, where it enriches the reflection on the course of things and the fruit of human actions.
H1933B.portee: This verb reminds us that we are not fixed in our condition: we can become something else, change, transform. The Bible speaks of becoming, of passage, of what happens — all realities that call for our faith. It also invites us to reflect on the real effects of our actions and work: "what comes of it?" — a profound question for our faith life, which brings us back to the One who gives meaning to all our efforts.

sens: To occur, to happen, to take place
To come into existence, to be born, to form
To become, to transform into something
To be in a state, to find oneself in a condition
To look, to observe (secondary meaning)
To want, to desire (with participle)
H1934.detail:
1. The word primarily designates an event that occurs: something happens, arises in the course of time. In Daniel 2:28, the prophet interprets the king's dream and announces what "will happen" in the future: kingdoms will appear one after another.

2. It also describes the emergence, the beginning of something new: an act that is born, a situation that forms. This can concern the appearance of a vision or a reality.

3. The word expresses transformation, the passage from one state to another: one becomes something different. In Daniel 2:42, the text states that the kingdom will be "partly" strong and "partly" fragile, showing a succession of distinct states.

4. In certain contexts, it simply designates the fact of being in a given state or condition, of finding oneself in such or such a situation.

5. The word can also mean "to look" or "to observe": in Daniel 2:34, the king "was looking" at the statue, he was a spectator of a vision unfolding.

6. With a participle of will, it expresses wanting or desiring: in Daniel 5:19, the king "wanted" to have some killed and let others live, showing the exercise of his authority.
H1934.origine: This Aramaic verb comes from a very ancient root, common to several Semitic languages, which fundamentally expresses the idea of becoming, being, existing. It is close to the Hebrew "hayah" (היה), the verb "to be" par excellence, which appears thousands of times in the Old Testament. The Semitic root evokes a passage from one state to another, a transformation or actualization of being. In Aramaic, this verb plays the same central role as "to be" in French to express existence, appearance, and change.
H1934.emploi: This verb is one of the most frequent in biblical Aramaic: it appears 54 times, almost exclusively in the books of Ezra and Daniel, which are portions of the text written in Aramaic. In the book of Ezra, it reports the historical events that happen: the work on the Temple continues (Ezra 5:5), the orders of the king are given. In Daniel, particularly in chapters 2 to 7, the verb animates the narratives of visions and dreams: the statues that appear, the beasts that arise, the walls that collapse. The meaning slightly changes according to the context: sometimes it emphasizes the simple succession of facts ("it happened"), sometimes it accentuates the miraculous or prophetic nature of an appearance. With participles, particularly in Daniel 5:19, it can express a continuous disposition or will.
H1934.portee: This verb reminds us that God masters the course of events and transformations in history. When Daniel interprets the royal dreams and announces what "will happen," he affirms divine knowledge of the future and His sovereignty over kingdoms. For the believer, this word emphasizes that nothing is by chance: God sees what happens and what must happen, and He reveals His plan to His servants. It is an invitation to trust His prophetic Word.

sens: The brilliance, the visible splendor of a person or thing that commands respect
The honor, dignity, authority recognized in someone
The magnificence, the impressive greatness of God manifested in His creation and acts
The imposing appearance, the majestic demeanor of one who inspires respect
H1935.detail:
1. The word primarily designates visible splendor, the brilliance that strikes the eyes: it is the impressive and radiant exterior aspect of a person or creation. Job speaks of the majesty of the north "made bright like gold" (Job 37:22), an image of light and beauty.

2. It also signifies the honor and dignity attributed to someone, their social weight and authority. Moses must give Joshua a share of his "dignity" so that Israel respects him (Numbers 27:20) — this is not magical power, but the official recognition and prestige necessary to govern.

3. The majesty of God is His impressive greatness revealed in the order of the world and history: "His glory is great because of Your help" (Psalms 21:6), and His work is nothing but "splendor and magnificence" (Psalms 111:3). It is the divine power perceived with fear and wonder.

4. The word can finally describe the imposing, almost majestic demeanor of a creature: the branches of restored Israel will have "the magnificence of the olive tree" (Hosea 14:6), a proud and imposing beauty.
H1935.origine: The Hebrew word הוֹד comes from a root that evokes the idea of radiance and distinction. It is related to other Hebrew terms expressing glory and splendor. The basic image is that of visible brilliance: what shines and catches the eye, what stands out for its beauty and presence. In the Bible, this word is often associated with God and His works, particularly to express His manifest and impressive greatness.
H1935.emploi: This word appears 24 times in the Hebrew Bible, especially in the Psalms (where God is praised for His majesty), in the wisdom books (Job), and among the prophets. In the Psalms, majesty is usually that of God or His work: "His work is nothing but splendor and magnificence" (Psalms 111:3). It can also refer to human honor — Moses passes his dignity to Joshua (Numbers 27:20), and the king bears the brilliance (Psalms 21:6). Among the prophets, it takes on a dimension of divine power manifested: Isaiah speaks of the "majestic" voice of the Lord, thunder and judgment (Isaiah 30:30). The word always emphasizes the impression of greatness, authority, and brilliance that cannot be ignored.
H1935.portee: Recognizing the majesty of God is to admire Him in His creation and His acts, to accept His absolute authority, and to live in reverence toward Him. This word invites the believer to go beyond religious routine and to contemplate the greatness that imposes itself on all our senses. For leaders, majesty reminds us that all power and honor derive from God alone and must be exercised with responsibility and fear of Him.

sens: man of the tribe of Asher
son of Zophah
descendant of Asher during the divided monarchy
H1936.detail: 1. Hod is a man who belongs to the tribe of Asher, one of the twelve tribes of Israel. He is a member of the family of Asher, whose father is Zophah. 2. Hod is a descendant of Asher mentioned in the genealogy of Asher, where he is cited among the sons of his father Zophah and among many brothers: Suah, Harnepher, Shual, Beri, Imrah, Betser, Shamma, Schilscha, Jithran, and Beera (1 Chronicles 7:37). 3. He lived during the time of the divided monarchy in Israel, but no events of his life are reported; he is known only through this genealogy that lists the descendants of Asher and shows the structure of the families of this tribe.
H1936.origine: The name Hod means "splendor" or "brilliance" in Hebrew. This name expresses the idea of glory or brightness, qualities valued in biblical culture. The name is borne by several descendants of Asher, reflecting the importance of tribal genealogies in Israelite tradition.
H1936.emploi: Hod is mentioned only once in the entire Bible, in 1 Chronicles 7:37. He appears in a detailed genealogy of the descendants of Asher. The context is purely genealogical: the text lists the sons of Zophah, of whom Hod is a part. No act, no word, no event concerning Hod is reported; his name simply appears as a link in a genealogical chain intended to establish the history and descent of the tribe of Asher.

sens: Leader of a Levitical family upon returning from exile
H1937.detail: 1. Hodva is a leader of a Levitical family who returns from Babylonian captivity with the people of Judah. The text in Nehemiah 7:43 mentions him as an ancestor of the sons of Joshua and Kadmiel, of whom seventy-four returned to Jerusalem. It is one of the names of the same person, also called Hodaviah or Judah in other lists of the return from exile.
H1937.origine: The name Hodva means "Praise of the Lord" in Hebrew, composed of hod ("glory, splendor, praise") and vah (abbreviation of the name of God, Yahweh). It is a common theophoric name in Israel, expressing gratitude towards God. It designates several individuals during the time of exile and return.
H1937.emploi: Hodva appears only once in the Bible, in Nehemiah 7:43, in the list of Levites who returned from captivity in Babylon under the leadership of Zerubbabel and Nehemiah. This man was the head of a branch of the Levitical family; seventy-four of his descendants are listed among those who were able to return to Jerusalem. These lists of the ancestors of the returning families show the importance of preserving tribal lineage and the order of Levitical worship, essential for the restoration of the temple and divine service.

sens: Man of the tribe of Judah, son of Eljoenaï
H1938G.detail: Hodavia is a character mentioned only once in the Bible, in the genealogical record of the first book of Chronicles. He is presented as the son of Eljoenaï and is part of a sibling group of seven children named in that same verse. This man lived during the time of the divided monarchy in Israel. Although his name is significant — it means "praise Jehovah" — the Scriptures provide no details about his life, actions, or role. He is simply listed among the descendants of the royal house of Judah, suggesting his belonging to an important lineage, but he remains a minor figure whose only written testimony is this genealogical mention.
H1938G.origine: The name Hodavia means "praise Jehovah" (hô = "praise" and Jah = "Jehovah"). It is a theophoric name, meaning it carries the name of God and expresses a religious action or attitude. Like many Hebrew names, it reflects an aspiration or confession of faith: parents who gave this name to their child wished for his life to be a praise to the Lord.
H1938G.emploi: Hodavia appears only once in the Holy Scriptures, in 1 Chronicles 3:24, in a genealogical list of David's descendants. He is listed as one of the seven sons of Eljoenaï. The context is that of the royal chronicles of Judah, where the generations succeeding after the Babylonian exile are recorded. His unique mention shows that the author of the book of Chronicles aimed to document the complete lineage of the house of David, even for later generations of which no memorable deeds are reported.

sens: Man of the tribe of Manasseh, head of a family during the divided monarchy
H1938H.detail: Hodavia is a head of a family from the tribe of Manasseh, living at a time when the kingdom of Israel was divided between Judah and Northern Israel. In 1 Chronicles 5:24, he is presented alongside other leaders of the paternal houses of Manasseh, all described as valiant and renowned men, responsible for their respective clans.
H1938H.origine: The name Hodavia means "Praise Jehovah" — composed of the imperative "praise" and the divine name. It is a typical theophoric name from Israel, which expresses praise to the Lord and reflects the piety of Israelite families during this period.
H1938H.emploi: Hodavia appears only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 5:24, where he is listed among the military and administrative leaders of the tribe of Manasseh established east of the Jordan. He is included in a genealogical list that enumerates the valiant men recognized as heads of their paternal houses, showing his importance in the tribal and political structure of his time.

sens: Benjamite of the Return from exile, son of Assenua
H1938I.detail: Hodavia is a man from the tribe of Benjamin mentioned only once in the Bible, during the Return from exile after the Babylonian captivity. He appears as the ancestor of Meshullam, who himself is the father of Sallu. These three men are listed among the heads of families of Benjamin who resettled in Jerusalem. The passage in 1 Chronicles 9:7 cites him as "son of Assenua," thus establishing his lineage and status in the post-exilic genealogy.
H1938I.origine: The name Hodavia means "praise the Lord" (composed of the imperative "praise" and the divine name "Yah"). This type of theophoric name, containing the name of God, was common in Israel to express a promise or prayer. The name reflects the conviction that praising God was at the heart of family faith.
H1938I.emploi: Hodavia appears only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 9:7. He is included in a genealogical list of the Benjaminite families who returned from Babylonian exile to Jerusalem. These genealogical lists in the book of Chronicles served to establish the identity of families authorized to settle in Jerusalem and participate in the life of the rebuilt community. Although little known, Hodavia represents one of the noble families of Benjamin that participated in the restoration of Judah after the exile.

sens: Head of a Levitical family of the return from exile
H1938J.detail: Hodavia is a Levite mentioned in Ezra 2:40 as the ancestor of an important family that returned from captivity in Babylon. His name designates a lineage of seventy-four descendants who participated in the reconstruction of the temple in Jerusalem after the exile.
H1938J.origine: The name Hodavia means "Praise Jehovah" — it combines the imperative "praise" (hôdu) and the divine name "Jah" (Yah). It is a typical name from the post-exilic period, expressing trust and gratitude towards God at the time of return.
H1938J.emploi: Hodavia appears only once in the Bible in Ezra 2:40, in the list of Levites who returned from captivity under the leadership of Zerubbabel. This name also appears in Nehemiah 7:43 (spelled Hodevah) in a parallel list. The family of the sons of Hodavia numbered seventy-four members and played a role in the service of the restored temple. There are also namesakes (one from Manasseh and one from Benjamin) in the genealogies of Chronicles, but the Hodavia of the return community is the most historically significant.
H1938J.portee: This name reminds us that the return from exile was not the work of a few isolated individuals, but the result of the efforts of entire families, especially the Levites who had preserved the religious heritage. Hodavia symbolizes the continuation of praise to God despite the ruptures of history.

sens: One of the Levites who explained the law during the restoration of Jerusalem after the exile
H1941G.detail: Hodija is a Levite (a member of the priestly tribe of Levi) who appears three times in the book of Nehemiah, during the time of the return from exile and the reconstruction of Jerusalem (around the 5th century B.C.). In Nehemiah 8:7, he is mentioned among those who "explained the law to the people" during a great assembly where Ezra read the Torah. In Nehemiah 9:5, he is counted among the Levites who led the prayer and called the people to bless the Lord. In Nehemiah 10:10, he seals the covenant of the people with God. Thus, he was a respected spiritual leader of that time.
H1941G.origine: The name Hodija means "my majesty is the Lord" or "my splendor is Jehovah": it expresses the belief that the glory of the one who bears it comes from God Himself. In Ezra 3:9, this man is also called Judah (Yehoudah), suggesting that Hodija was a nickname or a variant of the same name. This nickname emphasizes the prominent role that God confers on the one who bears it.
H1941G.emploi: Hodija appears three times in the accounts of the return from exile and the restoration of the temple under Ezra and Nehemiah (around 458-432 B.C.). There may be several people bearing this name at the same time. He is presented as a leading Levite: he explains the law to the people (Nehemiah 8:7), participates in solemn prayers and the blessing of the people (Nehemiah 9:5), and signs the sacred covenant between the people and God (Nehemiah 10:10). His name regularly appears alongside important figures like Joshua, Bani, and Sherebiah, confirming his authority in the religious community of the return.
H1941G.portee: Hodija embodies the crucial role of the Levites after the exile: instructing the people, leading them to prayer and obedience to God's Law. His example shows that the spiritual renewal of a community relies first on the knowledge and teaching of God's Word, as well as on the commitment of religious leaders to guide the people in the covenant with the Lord.

sens: Levite during the time of Ezra and Nehemiah
H1941H.detail: Hodija is a Levite who lived during the time of the exile and the return to Jerusalem, alongside Ezra and Nehemiah. He appears in the list of the leaders of the people who sealed the covenant with God after the restoration of the temple (Nehemiah 10:13).
H1941H.origine: The name Hodija means "my majesty is the Lord": it is a statement of faith in Hebrew, composed of "hod" (majesty, glory) and "Yah" (abbreviation of the divine name). This name reflects the piety of the Levites who served God during the return from exile.
H1941H.emploi: Hodija is mentioned only once in the Bible, in Nehemiah 10:13, where he is listed among the Levites who signed the solemn covenant made after the restoration of Jerusalem. He was a man of spiritual responsibility, participating in the people's commitment to God and His Law.

sens: Levite who affixed his seal to Nehemiah's covenant
H1941I.detail: Hodija is a Levite mentioned only once in the Bible, in Nehemiah 10:18. At this time of the Exile and the Return, after the reconstruction of the Temple, Governor Nehemiah gathered the people to renew the covenant with God. The leaders of the people, the priests, and the Levites affixed their seal to this document, committing to uphold the Law of Moses. Hodija is among those Levites who publicly testify to this commitment.
H1941I.origine: The name Hodija means "my majesty is Jehovah" or "God is my majesty". It combines the Hebrew "hôd" (honor, majesty) and the divine "Yah" (short form of God's name). This type of theophoric name (containing the name of God) was common among the Hebrews and expressed the faith of the father who named his son.
H1941I.emploi: Hodija is mentioned only once in Nehemiah 10:18. At this time of the Return from Exile (around 445 B.C.), Nehemiah organizes a great ceremony where the main leaders of Jerusalem solemnly commit to following the Law. Hodija represents the Levites, those Temple servants responsible for teaching the Law and administering worship. His name appears in a long list of signatories, showing the collective importance of this moment of national covenant renewal.

sens: Evil desire, covetousness, or malicious intent
Misfortune, ruin, destruction that befalls someone
Devastation, damage
Trap, imminent disaster
H1942.detail:
1. The word primarily denotes a desire turned towards evil: malice, wickedness, the intention to harm others. In Psalms 52:9, the man who "triumphs in his malice" is one who boasts of his evil plans and unjustly acquired wealth.

2. By extension, it describes the misfortune, ruin, and destruction that result — not only as intention but as a reality experienced. In Job 6:2, Job asks that "all his calamities" be weighed, speaking of the overwhelming burden and concrete suffering that befalls him.

3. The word also evokes the idea of devastation and damage: something that destroys, that ravages. In Job 30:13, the adversaries "work towards his ruin", literally they plow his destruction.

4. Finally, it designates the trap, the imminent disaster from which one must guard oneself or seek protection. In Psalms 91:3, God delivers from traps and destructive calamities.
H1942.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root expressing the idea of desire, covetousness, with a negative connotation: a desire that torments, that destroys. The root is related to the image of a breach, a void that draws in. As with many Hebrew words, the meaning evolves from the inner feeling (the evil desire) to its visible effects (the ruin it causes).
H1942.emploi: This word appears 16 times in the Old Testament, primarily in Psalms and Proverbs, as well as in Job. It is used to describe either the malicious intent of enemies (Psalms 38:13, 52:9) or the misfortunes and sufferings endured by the righteous (Job 6:2, Psalms 57:2). Proverbs uses it to warn against the malice of the wicked (Proverbs 10:3, 11:6). Throughout all these uses, the word oscillates between malice as sentiment and destruction as consequence, uniting in a single reality the voluntary evil and the suffering evil.
H1942.portee: This word reminds the believer that malice, the desire to harm others, is never isolated: it engenders ruin and destruction. For the one who suffers, it names what burdens them, validating their distress before God. For the one tempted by malice, it warns of the consequences. Finally, turning to God against these calamities (as in Psalms 57:2) affirms that only God can protect us from destruction.

sens: A disastrous event, a sudden calamity that overwhelms a person or a people
Ruin, destruction that falls unexpectedly
A chain of successive misfortunes, an accumulation of hard blows
H1943.detail:
1. Calamity is primarily a negative event that occurs without warning. In Isaiah 47:11, the prophet announces to the kingdom of Babylon: "Calamity will come upon you, without you seeing the dawn" — meaning that disaster will strike suddenly, with no possibility of avoiding or foreseeing it. The word evokes something that falls from the sky, quick and inevitable.
2. This calamity takes the form of ruin, of concrete destruction: "Destruction will come upon you all at once, unexpectedly" (Isaiah 47:11). The word paints a picture of collapse, of a complete loss of what one possessed.
3. In Ezekiel 7:26, the prophet describes a succession of calamities: "Calamity comes upon calamity, noise follows noise" — the image is that of an avalanche, where hard blows accumulate without respite, plunging the people into disarray and helplessness.
H1943.origine: The Hebrew word הֹוָה (havah) is formed from the root havah which means "to fall," "to strike down," or "to come suddenly." The starting image is therefore that of something that falls or descends upon you without warning. This is why the word carries the idea of unexpected and inevitable calamity, an event that imposes itself from the outside.
H1943.emploi: The word appears twice in the Hebrew Bible, both in the prophets (Isaiah and Ezekiel). In Isaiah 47:11, it describes the judgment that God brings upon Babylon: a sudden calamity that will destroy it despite all its efforts to avert it. In Ezekiel 7:26, it depicts the chaos that invades Jerusalem at the time of the siege: calamity upon calamity, an accumulation of disasters that leaves the people without counsel and without hope. In both cases, the word is set in a context of divine judgment: calamity is not random, but the consequence of unfaithfulness to God.
H1943.portee: This word reminds the reader that God's judgment on sin is real and can be sudden. It invites spiritual vigilance and repentance, for the calamity described by the prophets is never inevitable: it is always God's response to unfaithfulness, and it can be avoided by returning to Him. For those who walk with God, this word also shows that God controls all events and uses them to call His people back to Him.

sens: King of Hebron at the time of Israel's conquest of Canaan
H1944.detail: Hoham is a Canaanite king who reigns over the city of Hebron at the time when Joshua leads the Israelites in the conquest of Canaan. He appears in Joshua 10:3, where Adoni-Zedek, king of Jerusalem, calls him to unite with him and four other Canaanite kings to fight against Joshua and the Israelites who threaten their dominion.
H1944.origine: The name Hoham literally means "he whom Jehovah pushes" or "whom Jehovah impels." It is composed of the divine element (Ho) and a term indicating the action of pushing or impelling. It is a typical name of Canaanite kings from this period.
H1944.emploi: Hoham appears only once in the Bible, in Joshua 10:3. He is mentioned among five Canaanite kings who conspire against Joshua: Adoni-Zedek of Jerusalem, Hoham of Hebron, Piram of Jarmuth, Japhia of Lachish, and Debir of Eglon. This alliance shows how local kings attempt to resist together against the Israelite invasion, but the biblical context suggests that this attempt will fail.

sens: Exclamation expressing pain, regret, or compassion in the face of death or loss
Announcement of divine judgment upon a city, a people, or a person
Prophetic warning of catastrophe or ruin
Urgent call to attract attention or exhort
H1945.detail:
1. In 1 Kings 13:30, it is a cry of mourning: "Alas, my brother!" — an interjection that expresses sadness in the face of death or misfortune that strikes someone close.
2. Among the prophets, particularly Isaiah and Jeremiah, "woe" announces God's judgment upon those who act wickedly. Isaiah 5:21 declares, "Woe to those who are wise in their own eyes," pointing to the guilty pride that attracts divine punishment.
3. The word prophesies concrete ruin: in Jeremiah 48:1, "Woe to Nebo, for it is ravaged!" — this is a judgment that falls upon a condemned city.
4. Sometimes, as in Isaiah 55:1 ("All you who are thirsty, come"), the interjection sharply calls someone to action or to heed an urgent appeal.
H1945.origine: This Hebrew interjection is a primitive cry, an onomatopoeia that expresses affliction. It belongs to a family of words related to lamentation and misfortune. Its prophetic use is rooted in the conviction that the prophet's words are not in vain: when he cries "woe," he pronounces a judgment that will come to pass. Ecclesiastes and the Psalms use related forms to express distress.
H1945.emploi: The interjection "woe" appears 37 times in the Segond 1910, mostly among the major prophets (Isaiah 26 times, Jeremiah 6 times, Ezekiel, Amos, Micah, Nahum, Habakkuk). It marks oracles of condemnation: against idolatrous cities, against unjust kings, against false prophets and those who oppress the poor. The prophets use it as an act of proclamation of judgment — it is not a mere lamentation, but a word that engages the future. In 1 Kings 13:30, the funerary context also reveals its use in personal mourning. In Isaiah, the accumulation of "woes" (Isaiah 5:8, 11, 18, 20, 21, 22; 10:1) creates a portrait of society that brings upon itself divine wrath.
H1945.portee: This prophetic interjection reminds the reader that God is not indifferent to injustice and pride. It warns: wicked acts, oppression, and lies do not go without consequences. It also exhorts to listen to the prophets who speak in the name of the Lord, whose word will be fulfilled. For the believer, it invites a fear of God and obedience.

sens: To move from one place to another, to walk
To be transported, led from one place to another
To be willing to depart, to set out
H1946.detail:
1. The fundamental meaning is that of movement: going from one place to another, walking or moving. This is the basic idea of the verb, which implies an ongoing action (Ezra 5:5: "until the reception" evokes the action of continuing, of moving forward in work).
2. The word also describes being transported or brought somewhere, often passively. The objects of the temple "transported to Babylon" and then "transported to the temple" (Ezra 6:5) do not move by themselves: they are carried, they are led.
3. Finally, it means being willing or ready to depart, manifesting a will or decision to set out. In Ezra 7:13, those who are "willing to depart" with Ezra express their consent to undertake the journey to Jerusalem.
H1946.origine: This Aramaic verb comes from the same root as the Hebrew הָלַךְ (halakh), which means "to walk" or "to go." It is a very common verb to express any movement, whether voluntary or imposed. The Aramaic form hukh belongs to the same family of words, retaining this fundamental idea of movement.
H1946.emploi: This verb appears only three times in the Aramaic Bible, all in the book of Ezra (5:5; 6:5; 7:13). In Ezra 5:5, it expresses the continuity of the reconstruction work of the temple; in Ezra 6:5, it describes the transport of sacred objects from Babylon to Jerusalem; in Ezra 7:13, it signifies the intention or willingness to undertake a journey. The context is always one of movements related to the restoration of the Jewish people and their worship.
H1946.portee: This verb reminds us that the path to God and to His house involves movement: to walk, to go, to set out. For the Christian, it evokes the idea of spiritual progression, of not remaining still in the face of God's call. The willingness to "depart" for Jerusalem (the temple, the holy place) illustrates the active commitment that faith requires.

sens: Absence of reason, common sense; mental disorder
Insensate behavior, action that contradicts wisdom
Stupid malice or wickedness devoid of intelligence
H1947.detail:
1. Foolishness primarily denotes a mental state: the absence of wisdom and reason. This is why Ecclesiastes speaks of knowing "wisdom, and knowing foolishness and folly" (Ecclesiastes 1:17) — it explores the two extremes of human thought. It stands in direct opposition to thoughtful wisdom.
2. This term also describes behavior: the way of acting when one abandons reason. Ecclesiastes seeks to understand "the folly of wickedness and the stupidity of foolishness" (Ecclesiastes 7:25), showing that foolishness guides senseless and harmful acts.
3. Finally, foolishness appears as a condition of the fallen human heart: "foolishness is in their heart during their life" (Ecclesiastes 9:3). It characterizes humanity far from God, engaged in paths that lead to death.
H1947.origine: This Hebrew word belongs to the family of the verb meaning "to act foolishly" or "to be unreasonable." Its original image is that of someone who wanders, who is mentally deranged. In the Greek Old Testament (Septuagint), it often translates the concept of moral folly — not mental illness, but the choice of the fool who rejects divine wisdom.
H1947.emploi: The word appears 4 times, exclusively in Ecclesiastes, the book where the Sage explores the meaning of existence. It is always contrasted with wisdom (Ecclesiastes 1:17; 2:12): the Sage seeks to understand both extremes. It also characterizes the moral state of the human heart (Ecclesiastes 9:3), revealing that without God, humanity remains in wandering. In Ecclesiastes 7:25, it is associated with wickedness, showing that foolishness produces evil.
H1947.portee: This word helps the believer recognize the true problem of humanity without God: it is not just ignorance, but the refusal of wisdom. It calls to actively seek wisdom rather than follow the paths of the fool. For the Christian, this emphasizes the importance of asking God for renewed understanding, capable of discerning good from evil.

sens: Loss of reason, mental disorder or unreasonable behavior
Stupid and senseless words or acts, contrary to wisdom
H1948.detail:
1. Folly is primarily the absence or loss of reason: it is when someone no longer thinks straight, when their mind wanders or becomes disordered. In Ecclesiastes 10:13, the preacher speaks of words that spring from the mouth of a fool: they begin in folly and end in "wicked folly," meaning they sink deeper into absurdity and lies.
2. Folly also denotes anything unreasonable: speaking without thinking, acting without wisdom, despising justice or righteousness. It is conduct that contradicts reason and the knowledge of God. What is said in folly has no foundation; it is mere wind and trouble.
H1948.origine: This word comes from the Hebrew root "hll" which evokes the idea of emptiness, lack, absence of meaning. Folly is literally a mental vacuity: the absence of what fills and orders the mind, namely wisdom and the fear of God. It stands in opposition to "hokhmah," wisdom, which fills and organizes thought.
H1948.emploi: The word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Ecclesiastes 10:13. The context is that of the "qohélet" (the Preacher), who observes and judges human existence. He notes that the words that come from a foolish mouth are themselves foolish: they begin in mental disorder and end in even graver absurdity. This remark highlights that folly is not just a disease of the mind; it is also a production: acts, words that testify to it.
H1948.portee: For the believer, this word reminds us of the importance of being mindful of what comes out of our mouth and heart. In Ecclesiastes, the Preacher invites us to recognize folly instead of sinking into it. It is an invitation to ask God for wisdom and to reject any behavior that opposes righteousness and common sense.

sens: to be troubled, disturbed, agitated in one's feelings
to be in turmoil, in commotion (crowd, city)
to make noise, to cause agitation
to show concern or distress
H1949.detail:
1. The word primarily describes an emotional disturbance or inner agitation: someone is shaken, loses their calm. In Ruth 1:19, when Naomi returns from the land of Moab, "the whole city was stirred because of them," meaning her unexpected presence provokes a strong reaction of astonishment and disturbance among the inhabitants.

2. It also refers to the tumult of a crowd or assembly that stirs together. In 1 Samuel 4:5, when the ark of the covenant enters the camp, "all Israel gave a great shout of joy, and the earth shook": the verb suggests collective effervescence, the movement and noise that result from it.

3. The word can simply denote the noise or agitation that ensues. In 1 Kings 1:45, after Solomon has been anointed king, "the city was stirred: that is the noise you have heard" – the collective emotion translates into an audible uproar.

4. Finally, it expresses personal concern or discomfort. In Psalms 55:3, the psalmist says: "I am agitated," showing how anxiety makes him restless and uneasy.
H1949.origine: The Hebrew verb הוּם (hum) fundamentally evokes the idea of tumultuous movement and noise. Its root expresses agitation, tumult, confusion. The word belongs to a family of Hebrew expressions that describe disorder and effervescence. It stands in opposition to tranquility and calm, and always suggests a disturbance, whether emotional, physical, or collective.
H1949.emploi: This verb appears five times in the Hebrew Bible, primarily to describe strong collective reactions. In Ruth 1:19, it is the emotion of a small town facing Naomi's unexpected return; in 1 Samuel 4:5, it is the tumultuous joy of Israel at the arrival of the ark; in 1 Kings 1:45, it is the urban effervescence after a major political event. The psalmist (Psalms 55:3) uses it to express his own personal distress. In Micah 2:12, it is the noise of a gathered crowd. The word always denotes a break in calm, a perceptible agitation, whether joyful, anxious, or simply tumultuous.
H1949.portee: This word reminds us that our collective and individual emotions – fear, joy, concern – have a concrete reality that manifests itself. It invites the reader to recognize that religious emotion, far from being only internal and silent, expresses itself freely and visibly. The joy before God's acts bursts forth and stirs the whole people; the anguish of the heart makes us restless and turbulent. It is an invitation to spiritual and emotional authenticity.

sens: son of Lotan
descendant of Seir the Horite
H1950.detail: Homam is a man mentioned only once in the Bible, in the midst of an ancient genealogy. He is the son of Lotan, who is himself the son of Seir the Horite — that is, a descendant of the ancient peoples who inhabited the region of Edom before the conquest by the Israelites (1 Chronicles 1:39).
H1950.origine: The name Homam means "confusion" in Hebrew. It designates a member of the dynasty of the Horites, these pre-Israelite populations who occupied the mountains of Edom.
H1950.emploi: Homam appears only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 1:39, in the genealogical list of the descendants of Seir the Horite. This genealogy enumerates the ancient inhabitants of the territory that would later become Edom, before the arrival of the Edomites (descendants of Esau). Homam is listed there as the son of Lotan, alongside his brother Hori. This genealogical context shows us the complexity of the peoples who populated the region long before the Israelite patriarchs.

sens: to consider something as easy or unimportant
to act without thinking of the consequences
to show boldness or carelessness in the face of a challenge
H1951.detail:
1. The word describes the attitude of one who considers something as light, without weight, without seriousness — as if it were not worth worrying about. In Deuteronomy 1:41, the Israelites, after hearing the report of the spies about the strength of the inhabitants of Canaan, still want to go up to attack: they make a "reckless plan" to go up the mountain, meaning they treat the danger as negligible.
2. By extension, the word expresses the action of one who undertakes something without weighing the risks, as if they did not exist. It is a form of lightness or carelessness in the face of a serious situation: the Israelites despise the warning and rush into battle without waiting for the Lord's command.
H1951.origine: The Hebrew root expresses the idea of what is light, easy, or unimportant. It evokes a dematerialization, a lightening of moral or physical weight. The context of Deuteronomy in particular shows how this "lightness" becomes a moral fault: treating lightly what God has commanded shows disrespect and disobedience.
H1951.emploi: The word appears only once in the Bible, in Deuteronomy 1:41. Moses recounts to the people how, after the alarming report of the spies about Canaan, the Israelites decided to go up to attack anyway, in an act of presumption. This unique occurrence shows the word in its strong moral sense: acting carelessly and proudly in the face of God's warnings is to "act recklessly." The historical context is that of the people's refusal to follow God's divine order for conquest at the prescribed time.
H1951.portee: This word warns every believer against the illusion that obstacles do not matter, or that our strength is sufficient if God does not accompany it. Treating divine counsel lightly or ignoring warning signs exposes one to failure and judgment. It reminds us that true wisdom consists in respecting God's order and timing, not in rushing impulsively and presumptuously.

sens: Material goods, money, possessions
The total assets of a person, their fortune
Value, price, esteem given to something
Enough, sufficiency (archaic sense)
H1952.detail:
1. The word primarily refers to the material goods one possesses: money, properties, anything that has economic value. In Proverbs 3:9, the believer is called to honor God "with your goods," meaning by offering a portion of their possessions to Him.
2. It extends to the entire fortune of a person, their complete assets. Psalm 112:3 promises that "wealth and riches" will fill the house of the one who fears the Lord.
3. The word can also express the value or esteem attributed to something. In Psalms 44:13, God is accused of not "valuing" His people highly: that is, treating them as if they had no worth.
4. Rarely, it means "enough" or "sufficient" in an interjection: this is an ancient and infrequent usage in the Bible.
H1952.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that evokes the idea of possessing, accumulating. It is related to the notion of what fills, what constitutes wealth. It is a concrete word: it paints the image of a house or a storehouse filled with goods, a treasure amassed.
H1952.emploi: The word appears 26 times in the Hebrew Bible, especially in Proverbs and Psalms, where it denotes fortune and prosperity. Proverbs constantly use it to speak of wealth as a sign of blessing or as a trap: wealth attracts friends (Proverbs 19:4), it can deceive the one who possesses it (Proverbs 13:7), or it comes from hard work (Proverbs 13:11). In Psalms, it is linked to the feeling of esteem and value: God values His people or takes away their worth. Ezekiel uses the term to describe the wealth of trading cities. The sense of "value" or "esteem" clearly appears in Psalms 44:13 and Song of Solomon 8:7, where wealth represents what is precious.
H1952.portee: This word invites the Christian reader to reflect on the true value of things and on their relationship to money. Proverbs warns against the illusion that wealth brings happiness or security: it can instead blind or harden the heart. But the Bible does not prohibit wealth; it places it under God's control and directs it towards generosity and honoring the Lord. It is a key to understanding the biblical tension between material prosperity and true spiritual values.

sens: son of Jeconiah, king of Judah
H1953.detail: Hoshamah is one of the sons of Jeconiah (also called Jehoiachin), the penultimate king of Judah before the fall of Jerusalem. He appears only once in the Bible, in the genealogy of the kings of Judah, listed among the brothers Malkiram, Pedaiah, Shenazzar, Jekamiah, and Nedabiah (1 Chronicles 3:18). His name means "the Lord hears" or "Jehovah listens," reflecting the faith of the parents in God's ability to answer prayers.
H1953.origine: The name Hoshamah is composed of two Hebrew elements: "Hosea" (or a related form) and "Yah" (the abbreviated divine name). It literally means "Jehovah hears" — an expression of trust in God. It is a typical theophoric name of Judean royalty, where parents gave their children names evoking the action or nature of God.
H1953.emploi: Hoshamah is mentioned only once in the entire Bible, in 1 Chronicles 3:18, in the genealogical list of the descendants of King Jeconiah. This genealogy is part of the official record of the kings and their descendants, preserved after the Babylonian exile. Hoshamah is part of the generation of the sons of Jeconiah, all of whom bore names evoking divine intervention — suggesting that despite the catastrophe of exile, the royal family maintained hope in God.

sens: Last king of the Northern Judah (Israel)
Son of Ela
King who reigned nine years over Israel in Samaria
H1954G.detail: Hosea is the name of the last king of the kingdom of Israel (Northern Judah). He ascended to the throne by overthrowing Pekah, son of Remaliah, during a conspiracy (2 Kings 15:30). He reigned for nine years over Israel, with Samaria as the capital (2 Kings 17:1). Under Hosea's reign, the kingdom of Israel lost its independence: first forced to pay tribute to Assyria (2 Kings 17:3), he later refused this vassalage and sought help from Egypt (2 Kings 17:4). The king of Assyria imprisoned him and conquered Samaria, taking the Israelites into captivity (2 Kings 17:6). Thus, with Hosea, the kingdom of the North comes to an end, and his captivity marks the end of Israel as an independent nation.
H1954G.origine: The name Hosea means "salvation" or "he who saves" in Hebrew. It is formed from the root that expresses the idea of deliverance and help. It is a name filled with hope, although the character who bears it did not save his kingdom from destruction.
H1954G.emploi: Hosea is mentioned eight times in the book of Kings, notably in 2 Kings 15:30, 17:1-6, and 18:1-10. The accounts focus on his rise to power (where he overthrows Pekah), his nine years of reign, his relations with Assyria (first as a vassal paying tribute, then in revolt), his failed diplomatic alliance with Egypt, his imprisonment, and ultimately the fall of Samaria and the captivity of the people of Israel during his reign. Hosea symbolizes the end of an era: he is the last king of the North before the dispersion of its inhabitants.
H1954G.portee: The story of Hosea illustrates how a kingdom that turns away from God loses its protection and independence. Although his name means "salvation," Hosea did not have the wisdom to seek God's help; instead, he turned to human powers (Egypt) and ended up in prison. His reign marks for Israel a historical and theological turning point: the end of national independence and the beginning of exile, a decisive moment when God seems to abandon His people — but from a biblical perspective, this abandonment is a consequence of the people's sin, not a failure of God.

sens: Leader of Ephraim under King David
Son of Azaziah
H1954H.detail:
1. Hosea is a leader of the tribe of Ephraim during the time of King David. He is mentioned as responsible for his tribe in the register of royal officials (1 Chronicles 27:20).
2. He is the son of Azaziah, which gives us his lineage within the people of Israel.
H1954H.origine: The name Hosea comes from Hebrew and means "salvation" or "he who saves." This same name was borne by several important figures in Israel's history: the prophet Hosea from the Northern Kingdom, one of the twelve minor prophets, and also the name given to Joshua, son of Nun, before his calling. It is a theophoric name, revealing the expectation of divine deliverance.
H1954H.emploi: This particular Hosea is mentioned only once in Scripture, in 1 Chronicles 27:20, where he appears in the list of tribal leaders and officials of King David. He is identified as the leader of Ephraim and the son of Azaziah. This mention places him in an administrative context: that of a trusted man of the king, responsible for the organization and representation of his tribe within the Israelite government.

sens: An Israelite leader during the Exile and return
H1954I.detail: 1. Hosea is an Israelite leader who appears only once in the Bible, in Nehemiah 10:23, among the signers of the covenant made with Nehemiah after the return from exile in Babylon. He is a secondary figure from this time of rebuilding the Jewish people.
H1954I.origine: The name Hosea comes from Hebrew and means "salvation" or "deliverance." It is a form of the Hebrew word that expresses the fundamental idea of divine help. Although this name carries a rich meaning (salvation), this character from Nehemiah is known only by his appearance in this list of signers.
H1954I.emploi: Hosea appears only once in Scripture, in Nehemiah 10:23, where he is listed among the Israelite leaders who solemnly seal the covenant with God and Governor Nehemiah after the return from exile. This mention situates him historically at the end of the 5th century B.C., at the time when the Jews were rebuilding Jerusalem and its temple. His name in this list suggests that he was a person of some importance in the community of that time.

sens: Prophet of Israel in the 8th century B.C.
Son of Beeri
Man whom God commanded to marry an unfaithful woman to symbolize Israel's unfaithfulness
H1954J.detail: 1. Hosea is a prophet sent by God to the Northern Kingdom (Israel) during the reign of Jeroboam II (8th century B.C.), at the same time that the kings of Judah Uzziah, Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah reign in the South. His name means "salvation" in Hebrew. 2. Hosea is the son of Beeri, as the text specifies from his first mention in Hosea 1:1. 3. To deliver a dramatic prophetic message about Israel's unfaithfulness to the Lord, God commanded Hosea to marry Gomer, an unfaithful woman, and to have children with her whose names (Jezreel, Lo-Ruhamah, Lo-Ammi) expressed divine judgment. This broken marital life became a living sermon: as Hosea suffered from his wife's unfaithfulness, God suffered from Israel's unfaithfulness.
H1954J.origine: The name Hosea (הוֹשֵׁעַ, ho-shéa) comes from the Hebrew root meaning "to save" or "to deliver." This same name was borne by other biblical figures, notably Joshua (also called Hosea in some contexts). The name expresses God's saving action, which is particularly significant for a prophet whose ministry aims to call Israel to repentance before judgment.
H1954J.emploi: Hosea is the prophet author of the book that bears his name in the Old Testament. The two uses provided present him at the beginning of his prophetic mission: first explicitly named in Hosea 1:1 as "Hosea, son of Beeri," and then immediately addressed by God in Hosea 1:2, who commands him to take a symbolic prophetic action. His ministry spans several decades of the 8th century B.C., and his book contains 14 chapters of prophetic messages to Northern Israel. Hosea primarily prophesies during the reign of Jeroboam II, a period of apparent material prosperity but serious spiritual and moral decline in Israel.
H1954J.portee: Hosea embodies God's faithfulness to His people despite their unfaithfulness. His painful marriage to Gomer, commanded by God, reveals how God loves Israel with unwavering tenderness and tenacity, even in the face of rejection and abandonment. For the Christian, Hosea shows that God uses the personal trials of prophets to teach deep spiritual truths, and that divine faithfulness persists even when the people turn away.

sens: Son of Nun, first leader of Israel after the conquest of Canaan
Prophet of the Northern Kingdom in the 8th century B.C.
King of Israel, nineteenth and last of the Northern dynasty
Leader of Ephraim during the time of King David
Israelite leader who sealed the covenant with Nehemiah
H1954K.detail: 1. Hosea is the original name of the son of Nun, who would become the great leader and conqueror of Israel; Moses renamed him Joshua, which means "the Lord saves" (Numbers 13:8, 13:16). 2. Hosea is also a prophet who spoke on behalf of God in the kingdom of Israel during the reign of Jeroboam II in the 8th century B.C., announcing divine judgment on the unfaithful people. 3. Hosea was also the king of Israel, the nineteenth and last monarch of the Northern Kingdom, before it was destroyed by the Assyrians. 4. A Hosea was also a leader of the tribe of Ephraim during the time of King David. 5. After the exile, a Hosea was among the Israelite leaders who signed the renewed covenant with Nehemiah.
H1954K.origine: The name Hosea (Hebrew הוֹשֵׁעַ) means "salvation" or "deliverance." It derives from a Hebrew root expressing the idea of saving or delivering. Moses changed this name to Joshua (יְהוֹשׁוּעַ), which literally means "the Lord saves," adding the divine name (Yah) to mark the particular destiny of this man he called to lead Israel.
H1954K.emploi: The name Hosea appears in three major contexts in Scripture. First, it is the original name of the son of Nun, whom Moses renamed Joshua before sending him to explore Canaan (Numbers 13:8); Moses wanted to emphasize that it is the Lord who would save the people through this leader (Numbers 13:16). Secondly, Hosea is the 8th-century prophet who wrote the eponymous book, marking the end of the twelve minor prophets. Thirdly, Hosea was the last king of Northern Israel before its fall. These different uses of the same name highlight the continuity of the theme of divine salvation throughout Israel's history.
H1954K.portee: The change of Hosea's name to Joshua by Moses teaches that true deliverance comes from the Lord alone, not from human strength or wisdom. This theme runs throughout Israel's history: from the conqueror whom God saved to the last king who fell due to unfaithfulness. Christians find this same promise in Jesus, whose Greek name (Ἰησοῦς) shares the same root as Joshua, manifesting that ultimate salvation comes from the Lord.

sens: Prince of Judah at the time of Nehemiah
Leader who participated in the dedication of the wall of Jerusalem
H1955G.detail:
1. Hosea is a prince or leader of Judah who lived at the time when the people returning from exile were rebuilding Jerusalem. His name means "the Lord has saved," reflecting the divine deliverance that Judah needed after the exile.
2. He is mentioned as one of those who walked at the head of a choir during the solemn dedication ceremony of the wall of Jerusalem, alongside half of the leaders of Judah (Nehemiah 12:32). This important participation shows his authority and role in the restoration of the people.
H1955G.origine: The name Hosea comes from a Hebrew root meaning "to save" or "to deliver." It is a theophoric name, meaning it includes the name of God (Yah for the Lord). The same name exists among other biblical figures, notably the prophet Hosea, but here it refers to a leader from the time of Nehemiah, well after the time of the prophet.
H1955G.emploi: Hosea appears only once in the Bible, in Nehemiah 12:32. He is presented as an important figure during the time of the rebuilding of the wall of Jerusalem under the governance of Nehemiah, probably in the fifth century B.C. His role is to lead one of the two choirs that went up on the wall for the dedication ceremony, indicating a recognized leadership position among the leaders of Judah.

sens: Military leader of Judah after the fall of Jerusalem
Father of Jezaniah (also called Azariah)
H1955H.detail: 1. Hosea is an important military leader who appears alongside Johanan, son of Kareah, after the destruction of Jerusalem by Nebuchadnezzar. He represents the authority of the Judean survivors and participates in the collective decisions of the people. 2. He is the father of Jezaniah, also named Azariah in the texts, a prominent figure who plays an active role in the events of this period. His son notably appears when the people reject the message of the prophet Jeremiah regarding Egypt.
H1955H.origine: The name Hosea means "the Lord has saved" in Hebrew, formed from "hôsha" (to save) and the divine name Yah. It is a common theophoric name in Israel, expressing trust in divine deliverance. Several people bear this name in the Scriptures, but these occurrences refer to the father of Jezaniah who lived during the time of Jeremiah.
H1955H.emploi: Hosea appears only twice in the Bible, both in Jeremiah 42 and 43. He is mentioned as one of the main military authorities alongside Johanan, son of Kareah, at the critical moment following the assassination of Gedaliah and the destruction of the kingdom of Judah. With his son Jezaniah (Azariah), he is among the men who oppose the prophetic word of Jeremiah and decide to flee to Egypt despite the prophet's warning. His role illustrates the resistance of the survivors to the revealed will of the Lord.
H1955H.portee: The testimony of Hosea and his son shows how, even among the leaders of the rescued people, unbelief can prevail. Their example invites the reader to consider the danger of rejecting the word of God out of fear of circumstances, even when it comes from an authentic prophet. It is a lesson on the necessity of trusting the Lord rather than human wisdom.

sens: son of Heman, Levite from the tribe of Levi
temple musician during the divided monarchy
H1956.detail: Hothir is a Levite from the tribe of the Kohathites, son of the musician and prophet Heman (1 Chronicles 25:4). He is one of Heman's thirteen sons, all destined for musical service in the temple under their father's direction. The name means "abundance" in Hebrew. He appears in the official list of choir leaders of the temple during the time of King David, where he is assigned to the twenty-first division of service (1 Chronicles 25:28).
H1956.origine: The name Hothir comes from Hebrew and literally means "abundance." It belongs to the Levitical family of the Kohathites, an important branch of the priesthood of Israel responsible for the musical and liturgical service of the temple.
H1956.emploi: Hothir is mentioned twice in the Scriptures, only in the first book of Chronicles. He first appears in the genealogy of Heman's sons (1 Chronicles 25:4), where thirteen sons are listed with their names. He is then cited in the organization of the temple service (1 Chronicles 25:28), where he receives the twenty-first lot of service with his sons and brothers, each receiving twelve men under his authority.

sens: State of one who dreams or dozes without true vigilance
Mental confusion, wandering
Inattention, lack of clarity
H1957.detail: 1. Daydreaming primarily refers to the state of one who dreams — not the nocturnal dream, but rather this intermediate state between sleep and wakefulness, where the mind wanders. In Isaiah 56:10, the watchmen of the people have "daydreams": they doze instead of watching, unable to fulfill their mission with vigilance. 2. The word more broadly evokes mental confusion, a wandering of the mind. It is the opposite of clarity and responsibility: one who has daydreams is not truly attentive to what is happening around them. 3. By extension, it also means inattention and lack of clarity in the face of dangers. The blind watchmen of Isaiah 56:10 can neither see nor act; they are lost in a kind of ineffective stupor.
H1957.origine: The Hebrew verb הָזָה comes from a root expressing the idea of letting go, of mentally wandering. It is related to the image of sleep and dream, which depicts a mind that no longer controls its thoughts. The word describes not just the simple act of sleeping, but the confused state that accompanies it.
H1957.emploi: This verb appears only once in the Bible, in Isaiah 56:10. The context is very clear: the prophet denounces the spiritual leaders of Israel — described as blind watchmen — who are unable to watch over the people. They have "daydreams"; they doze; they love to sleep. This is not a critique of natural sleep, but an accusation of indifference and spiritual negligence. The watchmen who should be vigilant are instead asleep and confused.
H1957.portee: This word warns the believer about the danger of spiritual stupor. Just like the watchmen in Isaiah, a Christian can slip from vigilance to daydreaming, from attention to faith to indifference. It is a call to remain awake, to stay aware of one's responsibility toward God and others. Spiritual daydreaming is a form of betrayal of the trust received.

sens: cry or sound of pain, complaint
expression of moral or physical suffering
written or prophetic lamentation
H1958.detail: 1. Groaning is the cry or sound made by someone who suffers, who groans in pain or sorrow. It is a sound of natural, spontaneous complaint. 2. More broadly, it is the expression of suffering, whether from the body or the heart: the pain of one who weeps or laments. In the vision of the prophet Ezekiel, the scroll unfolded before him bears written groanings, that is, words of lamentation and distress (Ezekiel 2:10). 3. In a prophetic context, groaning becomes a form of proclamation: it is the voice of one who reports the suffering and misfortune sent by God, particularly the message of judgment from the prophet.
H1958.origine: The Hebrew word הִי (hi) primarily expresses the natural sound of sorrow and pain. It belongs to the group of cries and laments, like its neighbors "complaint" and "mourning." The initial image is thus that of the human sound of suffering, one that spontaneously emerges from someone enduring misfortune.
H1958.emploi: This word appears only once in the Bible, in Ezekiel 2:10, in the vision where the prophet receives the scroll of his mission. The scroll simultaneously bears lamentations, complaints, and groanings — in other words, the entire range of cries of pain and misfortune that the prophet will have to proclaim to Israel. Groaning thus designates the emotional and prophetic content of the message: Ezekiel is not to announce good news, but to make heard the voice of suffering and divine judgment.
H1958.portee: For the Christian reader, this word reminds us that biblical prophecy is not an abstract or cold word, but carries within it the compassion and pain of God's heart in the face of His people's rebellion. The groaning written on the prophet's scroll invites us to listen to the Bible, including its difficult messages, not as a brutal condemnation, but as the call of a God who suffers from the sin of His people.

sens: Loud and piercing cry made by a crowd or group
Cry of joy, celebration
War cry, call to battle
H1959.detail:
1. The word primarily designates a powerful cry emitted collectively, particularly during grape harvests or harvests, a moment of intense community life. It is the noise and exclamation of the workers treading the grapes at the press, as seen in Jeremiah 48:33: "No longer do they tread wine in the presses with joy."
2. It can express joy and gladness, the cries of celebration that accompany bountiful harvests and times of peace. In Jeremiah 48:33 and 16:10, these joyful cries have disappeared from the land that has become desolate, showing that the word primarily evokes a sound of life and happiness.
3. The word is also used for the war cry, the call to battle or resistance: in Jeremiah 51:14, the enemies raise "war cries" against the city. It then expresses a collective threat and the tumult of battle.
H1959.origine: The Hebrew word הֵידָד comes from a root expressing a loud and piercing cry. It belongs to the family of onomatopoeias, that is, words that imitate the sound they designate. The word evokes the vibrant and repeated noise of a crowd, like the song or cry of workers responding to each other during the harvests.
H1959.emploi: The word appears five times in the prophets, almost always associated with the grape harvest and the harvest. In Isaiah 16:9-10 and Jeremiah 48:33, the prophet contrasts the joyful cries of the past with the silence of judgment: when God judges, the harvests cease and the joyful cries disappear. In Jeremiah 25:30, it is God Himself who raises cries against the earth, like the harvesters against the press—an image of His terrible anger. In Jeremiah 51:14, the enemies raise war cries. The word can therefore be joyful or threatening depending on the context.
H1959.portee: This word reminds us that joy, celebration, and joyful communion are blessings from God. When judgment comes, these cries fade away: it is a sign of mourning and desolation. Conversely, when God acts powerfully, including against His enemies, His action provokes a great cry—one of His own strength and justice unfolding.

sens: Song or hymn of worship to God
Musical expression of gratitude and divine glorification
H1960.detail:
1. The word designates a song of worship, a song by which one praises God. In Nehemiah 12:8, Mattaniah and his brothers were responsible for leading these "songs of praise" among the Levites of the temple: it was an official and solemn function, linked to worship and community religious life.
2. More broadly, it expresses the idea of sacred music, of voices raised together to glorify God. It is less an individual act than a communal practice, where the people or the temple servants united their voices to manifest their gratitude to the Lord.
H1960.origine: The word comes from the Hebrew root "yada" which means "to praise," "to give thanks," "to acknowledge." The word "huyydot" is therefore literally "praises," in the sense of songs or expressions of praise. This root is very frequent in the Psalms and the Old Testament to describe the act of praising God, whether spoken or sung.
H1960.emploi: The word appears only once in the Bible, in Nehemiah 12:8. It is used in the context of the restoration of the temple after the Babylonian exile, when the Levites resumed their liturgical functions. Mattaniah is presented as the choir leader or conductor of these songs of praise, which shows the importance of sacred music in the worship of the second temple. It is a term that emphasizes the solemn organization and order of the religious service of restored Jerusalem.
H1960.portee: This word reminds Christians of the essential role of praise and song in worship rendered to God. It shows that praising God is not a secondary or optional activity, but an important part of the communal life of the Church. Songs of praise, when they are true and sincere, are a way to publicly acknowledge the greatness of God and to build each other up together.

sens: To exist, to have reality
To occur, to happen, to arrive
To become, to transform into
To last, to subsist, to persist
To serve as, to function as
To take place, to be accomplished
H1961.detail:
1. To exist, to have reality: the word designates the simple fact of being, of possessing existence. In Genesis 1:2, the earth "was" formless and void: it existed, but without a definable form.
2. To occur, to happen, to arrive: an action or event that manifests suddenly. In 2 Samuel 13:1, "after this, what happened was": things occur in the course of time.
3. To become, to transform into: to pass from one state to another. In 2 Chronicles 13:9, the one who brought the prescribed offerings "became a priest": he changed status through this act.
4. To last, to subsist, to persist: to remain in time and space. Genesis 3:20 shows Eve who "became" the mother of all living: she established a lasting reality.
5. To serve as, to function as: to fulfill a function or role. In Genesis 1:15, the luminaries "serve" as lights: they exist for this specific reason.
6. To take place, to be accomplished: to materialize according to a divine plan. In Genesis 1:3 and 1:7, "and it was so": God's order is realized and takes shape.
H1961.origine: The verb haya is the most fundamental form of the verb "to be" in Hebrew. It draws its roots from the primitive verb that expresses raw existence and becoming. Words from the family include nouns like "hayim" (life) and "hayya" (living animal): all share this central idea of reality and movement. It is the most frequently used verb in the Hebrew Bible, as it also serves as an auxiliary to form compound tenses and passive forms, and to introduce narrative propositions.
H1961.emploi: This verb appears 3,133 times in the Hebrew Bible, making it the most used word. It animates the creation narrative in Genesis 1: each day, "and it was so" signals the fulfillment of the divine word. It introduces historical events: "it happened" opens important narratives (2 Samuel 13:1). It marks transformations and changes of state: someone "becomes" king, priest, or guilty. It also expresses duration: someone "remains" alive, "dwells" somewhere. Depending on the context, the same form can mean "to be," "to take place," "to become," or "to serve": its exact meaning always depends on the context and accompanying complements.
H1961.portee: Haya reminds the reader that everything exists according to God's will and that everything that happens, from the most mundane to the most astonishing, is accomplished in His plan. By reading "and it was so," we grasp that the universe is not the result of chance but of divine word. This verb invites us to recognize both the stability of what exists and the perpetual movement of history: nothing is fixed, everything unfolds according to the Lord's design. For the believer, it is an invitation to place trust in the one who brings into being what exists and who directs the course of events.

sens: asks for the explanation, the manner or means of an action
expresses embarrassment, inability in the face of a situation
H1963.detail: 1. The word poses a question about the manner: "How will I do it?" David asks regarding the ark of God (1 Chronicles 13:12). It is a practical inquiry: by what means, in what way to accomplish an action? 2. It can also express embarrassment or hesitation in the face of difficulty. Daniel wonders: "How can the servant of my lord speak to my lord?" (Daniel 10:17), in other words: I do not know how to dare, how to find the strength to do it. The word is not just a technical question, but sometimes a sign of perplexity or weakness in the face of what exceeds.
H1963.origine: It is a fundamental interrogative word from ancient Semitic. It comes from the root that expresses the idea of "seeking" or "examining." It is a simple tool of spoken language, like in modern French "comment," which poses any question related to the manner or state of things.
H1963.emploi: The word appears twice in the Hebrew Bible, always to pose a question. David uses it when he wants to bring the ark to Jerusalem but wonders by what means to proceed (1 Chronicles 13:12). Daniel employs it to express his inability to find the words or the dignity to address the Lord (Daniel 10:17). In both cases, it is a sincere, non-rhetorical question that reveals a real concern of the speaker.
H1963.portee: This simple word reminds us that prayer and pious action can give way to practical questions and doubts. David seeks how to honor God; Daniel does not know how to stand before Him. The Bible allows us this: to question God, to confess our perplexity or weakness, is an act of honesty and faith.

sens: The main building of worship in Israel, where the presence of God dwells
The palace of a king or a god, the royal dwelling
The nave of a religious building, the interior space of the sanctuary
The heavenly dwelling of God, the temple of heaven
H1964G.detail:
1. The temple is the great sanctuary built in Jerusalem for the worship of the Lord. It is where sacrifices were offered, where the ark of the covenant was kept, and where the priests performed their liturgical duties. Hannah comes to pray there at Shiloh (1 Samuel 1:9), and the foundations of the new temple rebuilt after the exile are solemnly laid (Ezra 3:10).
2. The word also designates a royal or divine palace, the royal dwelling of an earthly or heavenly sovereign. The expression "palace of the Lord" in Psalm 29:9 evokes the majesty of God reigning in His heavenly domain.
3. Inside the temple, the word can specifically refer to the nave or the great hall, the main space of the religious building. The columns erected "before the temple" in 2 Chronicles 3:17 mark the entrance of this imposing structure.
4. The word also refers to the heavenly temple, the eternal dwelling of God in the heavens, of which the earthly temple was only the image and shadow. Jonah, swallowed by the fish, cries out to "your holy temple" (Jonah 2:5), that is, to the presence of God in the heavens.
H1964G.origine: The Hebrew word hekhal fundamentally designates a large house or an imposing building, probably borrowed from the architectural vocabulary of neighboring kingdoms. It comes from a root evoking solidity and magnitude. The same word applies to the palaces of kings (such as those of David or Solomon) and to the temple, as the temple is designed as the "house of God," His royal dwelling among men. The Bible reuses this word to speak of the heavenly temple, showing that the earthly temple reflects the heavenly reality.
H1964G.emploi: This word appears 52 times in the Old Testament, mainly in the historical books (Kings, Chronicles), the Psalms, and the prophets. It primarily designates Solomon's temple in Jerusalem, built as the central sanctuary of Israelite worship; then, after the destruction and exile, the temple rebuilt under Ezra. The usages show that the temple is not just a physical place, but the seat of divine presence: that is why the prophets see visions there (Isaiah 6:1, Ezekiel 8:16), why people plead with God there (Psalms 5:8, 27:4), and why its profanation or destruction is a grave act. The word also extends to the ideal or heavenly temple, depicted by the prophetic visions of Ezekiel and the messianic promises of Zechariah.
H1964G.portee: The temple reminds the believer that God does not dwell far from him, but has established a visible place of His presence and worship on earth. It is a sign of His covenant with Israel and His desire to dwell among His people. Understanding that the earthly temple reflected a heavenly reality helps the Christian grasp that true worship transcends walls and rituals: it is about encountering the living presence of God, as Jesus will teach when speaking of the temple of His body (John 2:19-21).

sens: Royal dwelling, residence of the king and his court
Imposing building where the king exercises his power and justice
Temple of God, holy house where He dwells among His people
Room or nave of a building (notably the temple of Ezekiel)
H1964H.detail:
1. The palace is primarily the king's dwelling, the place where he lives with his family and officers: it is a major, fortified, and prestigious construction. In 1 Kings 21:1, Ahab has a palace next to which is Naboth's vineyard, showing that the royal palace dominates the landscape of a city.
2. It is also the seat of royal power, the center from which the king governs and administers justice. Isaiah 39:7 speaks of the eunuchs taken to the palace of the king of Babylon: it is there that the closest servants of the sovereign live, controlling access to power.
3. By extension, the word designates the temple of Jerusalem as the dwelling of God and His royal house: God is the heavenly King who dwells in His sanctuary, like a monarch in His palace. That is why the temple is called the palace of God.
4. Finally, it can designate a part of a building, a room or a nave, particularly in the vision of Ezekiel's temple, where this term describes the different spaces of the holy house.
H1964H.origine: The word comes from a root that evokes what is spacious, large, extended. In Hebrew, the palace is primarily the building of royal power, the most imposing known in antiquity. When it was desired to speak of the dwelling of God, the same word was used: God, the supreme King, dwells in a heavenly palace, His temple being its earthly image. The word applies to both human palaces (those of the kings of Israel, Judah, Babylon) and to the house of the Lord.
H1964H.emploi: This word appears a dozen times in the Hebrew Bible, almost always in the singular. It regularly designates the palaces of the kings of Israel, Judah, and foreign powers (notably Babylon). Isaiah and Hosea use it for the sumptuous constructions in which Israel places its trust, far from trusting in God alone. The word also applies to the temple of Jerusalem, the royal dwelling of God: Psalms 45:16 speaks of entering the palace of the king, an image of divine worship. In Ezekiel's visions, the word is found to describe the parts of the future temple, each called palace or sanctuary.
H1964H.portee: The word palace invites us to recognize God as the true King and His temple as the seat of His eternal authority. When the kings of Israel build their own palaces without first seeking the living God, they turn away from their true Lord. Contemplating the palace of God is to submit to His royalty and find in Him the security and stability that human palaces can never offer.

sens: The house of God, a building dedicated to His worship
The large central hall of a temple, the nave where the divine service takes place
The royal palace, the residence of an earthly king
By extension, the heavenly dwelling of God, His eternal sanctuary
H1964I.detail:
1. The Hebrew word hékhal primarily refers to the temple in Jerusalem, the house built for God to dwell among His people and receive the worship due to Him. In 1 Kings 6:3, we see the porch in front of the "temple" of the house of the Lord.
2. More specifically, hékhal can refer to the main large hall of the temple, its central nave, distinct from the inner sanctuary or its dependencies. Ezekiel 41:1 and 41:4 clearly show this: it is the measurable part of the temple that the prophet sees in vision, before the most holy place.
3. The word also applies to royal palaces, as in biblical times the king and the temple shared similar architecture: hékhal is the residence of an earthly sovereign.
4. By analogy and spiritual elevation, hékhal refers to the heavenly dwelling of God, His eternal and invisible sanctuary, the model of which the earthly temple is only a figure.
H1964I.origine: The word hékhal comes from an ancient root meaning "palace" or "great house." It designates any building of prestige and importance: royal palaces, temples of gods. The same root is found in other ancient Near Eastern languages, where it always evokes a large hall or a royal dwelling. In Hebrew, the word belongs to the vocabulary of prestige and sacredness.
H1964I.emploi: The word hékhal appears twelve times in the Hebrew Bible. It is mainly used in 1 Kings 6, during the description of the temple built by Solomon: the dimensions of the porch, the nave, the pillars, and the doors are measured. It appears extensively in Ezekiel 41, in the vision of the future temple that the prophet sees in captivity: here too, the nave, the sanctuary, and the ornaments are measured and described. The context is always that of an architectural description or a prophetic vision. The word never designates the people or an immaterial aspect of worship, but always the physical structure of the holy place.
H1964I.portee: This word reminds the reader that God is not a distant abstraction, but that He desired a concrete, visible place where His people can meet and serve Him. The temple is the heart of Israel's religious life. Understanding hékhal also helps to grasp that Ezekiel's visions are not fantasies: they describe a real spiritual architecture, based on sacred geometry and form. For the Christian, this word opens up to the reality of heaven, the true dwelling of God that the earthly temple only foreshadowed.

sens: Religious building dedicated to the worship of the true God
Religious building dedicated to the worship of idols
Palace or royal dwelling
H1965G.detail:
1. The temple is primarily the house of God, the place where Israel meets Him and offers official worship. In the provided usages, it refers to the temple in Jerusalem, which Nebuchadnezzar plundered and from which the sacred vessels were taken to Babylon (Ezra 5:14, Daniel 5:2). It is a physical building with sacred objects, valuable utensils that belong to it.
2. The word also applies to the temples of pagan deities, such as the temple in Babylon (Ezra 5:14). It designates the same type of construction — a place of worship — but dedicated to false gods. The structure is the same; only the God honored there changes.
