3. By extension, héikhal can also mean palace or royal dwelling, as it is a large building of prestige. However, this usage is very rare in the provided texts; the main meaning remains that of a sacred temple.
H1965G.origine: The word héikhal comes from a root that expresses the idea of grandeur and splendor. It designates an imposing, majestic building, worthy of hosting the divine or royal power. The word appears particularly in accounts after the Babylonian exile, especially in the books of Ezra and Daniel, where it recalls the drama of the plundered temple and its restoration.
H1965G.emploi: This word appears 5 times in the provided texts, all in contexts of exile and restoration (Ezra and Daniel). It always refers either to the temple in Jerusalem or the temple in Babylon. The recurring mention of the vessels taken from the temple in Jerusalem and brought to the temple in Babylon (Ezra 5:14, Daniel 5:2-3) shows how the term marks religious identity: a temple is a place of identity, of divine or supposed presence. The meaning does not vary — it is always a place of worship — but the theological stakes change: the temple in Jerusalem is that of the living God, while the temple in Babylon is that of idols.
H1965G.portee: The temple reminds the reader that God wanted a terrestrial dwelling among His people, a concrete place to meet Him. But it is also a place that can be profaned and destroyed — exile shows that the temple is not inviolable. For the Christian, this speaks to the reality of divine presence and the necessity to respect it; in the New Testament, this presence transfers from the stone edifice to the body of Christ and to the Church.

sens: Royal residence, the dwelling of the king and sovereign
Building where the court and royal dignitaries live, where the great affairs of the kingdom are decided
H1965H.detail:
1. The word designates the residence of a king or sovereign — the place where he lives, where he manifests his power and authority. It is a magnificent, fortified, and guarded building, like the royal palace of Babylon where Nebuchadnezzar walks (Daniel 4:29), or the one where the king spends the night unable to sleep after the mysterious appearance of fingers writing on the wall (Daniel 6:18). The word evokes splendor, security, and power concentrated in one place.
2. More broadly, the palace is the seat of royal administration and power: it is where those who "eat the salt of the palace" (Ezra 4:14) reside, meaning those who live at the king's table and serve his interests. It is the center where the riches, secrets, and decisions of the kingdom are concentrated.
H1965H.origine: The Hebrew word hékhal comes from a root that evokes the idea of a large hall or an important structure. In Hebrew, the same word also applies to the temple in Jerusalem, as the temple was perceived as the "dwelling" of God, analogous to a royal palace — a place of sovereignty, majesty, and worship. The word thus emphasizes the importance and magnificence of a royal or sacred dwelling.
H1965H.emploi: The word appears five times in the Bible, only in the books of Ezra and Daniel, in contexts all related to Babylon and exile. In Ezra 4:14, it refers to the royal court from which those who eat the king's bread depend. In Daniel 4:4 and 4:29, it evokes the palace of Nebuchadnezzar where the king is "at ease" or "happy" before his reason is taken away. In Daniel 5:5, it is on the wall of the royal palace that the mysterious hand writes the judgment of Belshazzar. In Daniel 6:18, it is at the palace that the king withdraws, deeply troubled by the night spent fasting. Each time, the palace is the setting for royal life and the fate of kings in relation to God.
H1965H.portee: This word reminds us that even the greatest royal power, even the most magnificent palaces, cannot escape the authority of God. Nebuchadnezzar, "happy in his palace," becomes insane; Belshazzar sees the mysterious writing on the wall of his palace; the king who sleeps poorly in his palace can do nothing to protect Daniel. The palace, a symbol of human security, guarantees neither happiness nor protection when one disregards God.

sens: Morning star that shines before dawn
The one who shines, radiates light
Figuratively: the king of Babylon in his earthly glory
By extension: Satan, prince of darkness rebelling against God
H1966.detail:
1. The word primarily designates the morning star, this shining star that appears before sunrise and guides travelers — it is the brightest celestial body of the night (Isaiah 14:12).
2. More broadly, it refers to one who shines, radiates, dazzles by his splendor: the image evokes the brilliant clarity of a heavenly light.
3. In Isaiah 14, the prophet describes the king of Babylon using this royal image: he who rose like a shining star in the sky, surpassing the nations by his power and brilliance, now falls to the ground, brought low and humiliated.
4. Christian tradition has applied this passage to Satan himself, seeing in this king of Babylon a figure of the rebellious prince who sought to rise above God and was cast down — he who shone with beauty and power has become the prince of darkness.
H1966.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root meaning "to shine," "to radiate," "to give light": the basic image is that of light bursting forth and radiating. It is a common noun that naturally applies to the star that twinkles above our heads before dawn. Ancient Latin translations rendered this word as "Lucifer" (from Latin "lux" = light and "ferre" = to bear), a name that precisely designates the bearer of light.
H1966.emploi: The word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Isaiah 14:12, in the prophetic poem against the king of Babylon. The context is one of dramatic fall: this shining star, this son of the dawn who rose to the heavens, is cast down to the realm of the dead. This poetic image of the fallen king from his brilliance has served as a basis for theological reflection on the fall of Satan: Christian tradition has recognized in this passage a parallel with the revolt of the angel of light who transformed into the prince of darkness.
H1966.portee: This word reminds the reader that the beauty and splendor of human power, even the most dazzling, are fragile and subject to God's judgment. It also teaches that evil can cloak itself in deceptive splendor — Lucifer was not ugly, but resplendent before his fall. It is a warning against pride: he who rises above God, however brilliant he may be, is destined for humiliation.

sens: Son of Lotan, grandson of Seir, in the genealogy of the Edomites
H1967.detail: 1. Heman is a character mentioned only once in the Bible, at the time it lists the descendants of Seir the Horite. He is the son of Lotan and the brother of Hori (Genesis 36:22). He is a link in an ancient genealogy, that of the peoples who inhabited Canaan before the arrival of Israel.
H1967.origine: The name Heman means "the one who exterminates" or "destroyer" in Hebrew. This meaning suggests an image of strength or power, even if it is just a trait of the name. The biblical text offers a variant spelling of the same name: Homam (Genesis 36:22 in some manuscripts).
H1967.emploi: Heman appears only once in the entire Bible, in Genesis 36:22. This verse is part of the genealogies of Seir the Horite, the ancestor of the Horites who occupied the region of Edom. The context is purely genealogical: it is about tracing the families from whom Israel will inherit the lands. Lotan, Heman's father, is himself a character in this ancient genealogy.

sens: Renowned wise man during the reign of King Solomon
Levite musician and author of a psalm
H1968G.detail:
1. Heman is a wise and renowned man who lived during the reign of King Solomon, at the time of the united monarchy in Israel. King Solomon was famous for his extraordinary wisdom, and he was even reputed to be wiser than Heman and other men known for their wisdom: "He was wiser than any man, more than Ethan the Ezrahite, more than Heman, Calcol, and Darda, the sons of Mahol" (1 Kings 4:31). Heman belonged to a family of wise men, like his brothers Ethan, Calcol, and Darda.
2. Heman was also a Levite musician and a man of prayer. He is presented as the author of Psalm 88, titled "A Song of Heman the Ezrahite" (Psalms 88:1). This psalm is a prayer of lament addressed to God, and Heman was one of the appointed singers of the temple.
H1968G.origine: The name Heman means "faithful" in Hebrew, evoking the idea of someone who can be relied upon, who is trustworthy. The name appears in several biblical contexts and corresponds to different individuals in the history of Israel, reflecting the importance of the name in Israelite tradition.
H1968G.emploi: Heman is mentioned twice in the Segond. First in 1 Kings 4:31, where he is listed among the wise men of Solomon's time, presented as less wise than the king but renowned throughout the Middle East. Then in Psalms 88:1, where he is identified as the author of a lament psalm. According to ancient traditions, Heman was the son of Joel and the grandson of the prophet Samuel; he was a Levite of the tribe of Levi and served in the sanctuary as a musician and singer.

sens: Man of the tribe of Judah before the Israelite monarchy, wise man to whom Solomon was compared
Son of Joel, grandson of Samuel, Levite singer and author of Psalm 88
Seer in the kingdom of Israel
H1968H.detail:
1. Heman is a man of the tribe of Judah mentioned in 1 Chronicles 2:6 as the son of Zerah, famous for his wisdom. His name means "faithful" in Hebrew. Solomon himself, despite his great wisdom, was compared to Heman, which shows the esteem in which this sage was held: he was a reference point for wisdom in Israel even before the wisest king of all ascended the throne.

2. Heman is also the son of Joel, grandson of the prophet Samuel, and he held an important role in Israel's worship as a Levite singer. He was one of those responsible for leading praises in the temple. His role shows how music and singing were integrated into the official religious service of Israel.

3. Heman is also called a "seer," meaning someone who receives revelations from God. He composed Psalm 88, an intense prayer where the psalmist expresses his distress and feeling of abandonment, reminding us that even faithful servants of God experience deep suffering.
H1968H.origine: The Hebrew name Heman literally means "faithful." This name reflects the expected character of a wise person dedicated to God in the Old Testament. Faithfulness is a central virtue in Israel, particularly among those who serve the Lord. Several individuals bear this name in the Bible, but the most famous is the Levite singer associated with David's court.
H1968H.emploi: Heman primarily appears in 1 Chronicles 2:6 as one of the sons of Zerah of the tribe of Judah, counted among the great ancient sages. He is also the author of Psalm 88 and appears in the lists of Levite musicians responsible for the musical service of the temple under David. His importance in the Old Testament lies mainly in his role as a sacred singer and seer, that is, a transmitter of the divine word through music and prophecy. He embodies the function of wise-musician-prophet that characterizes certain privileged servants of the Lord in ancient Israel.
H1968H.portee: Heman shows us that God uses different types of servants: wise, musician, prophet. His psalm teaches us that faithfulness to God does not protect us from doubt or suffering; rather, it allows us to express our most honest cries before God. This is a valuable lesson for the Christian: authentic faith embraces doubt and distress as legitimate parts of our relationship with God.

sens: Chief of the singers of the temple during the time of the united monarchy
Levitical musician and composer of Psalm 88
Descendant of Samuel and son of Joel
Wise man to whom Solomon was compared
H1968I.detail:
1. Heman is a high-ranking musician in the service of the temple, responsible for the singers and musicians who perform the liturgical songs. He appears as early as 1 Chronicles 6:33 as "the singer, son of Joel, son of Samuel," indicating his position as the chief musician of worship.
2. He composes or is associated with Psalm 88, a psalm of lament and supplication, showing that the temple musicians were not merely performers but also inspired composers.
3. Heman is a member of the tribe of Levi and is a direct descendant of Samuel, which grants him spiritual authority in worship. He leads a large lineage of musicians (his sons Bukkijah, Matthania, Uzziel, and ten others) who assist him in his ministry.
4. The name Heman means "faithful" in Hebrew, and he is mentioned alongside Asaph and Jeduthun, the other two main music leaders; he is described in 2 Chronicles 35:15 as receiving orders from the king, a position of great trust.
H1968I.origine: The name Heman comes from Hebrew and means "faithful" or "believer." It reflects the trusted role Heman held with the king and in the service of the temple. He is a man from the tribe of Levi, dedicated to divine worship, and his genealogy traces back to Samuel, the great prophet and judge of Israel.
H1968I.emploi: Heman appears a dozen times in Chronicles (1 Chronicles 6:33; 15:17-19; 16:41-42; 25:1-6 and 2 Chronicles 5:12; 29:14; 35:15). He is always presented as the supreme leader of the singers and musicians of the temple, responsible for organizing the musical worship. His three eldest sons (Bukkijah, Matthania, and Uzziel) are also musicians, and he leads a total of seventeen musician sons. He collaborates closely with Asaph and Jeduthun, forming the trio of great music masters of Israel. The fact that he receives orders from the king (2 Chronicles 35:15) underscores his official status and the importance of musical worship in royal liturgy.
H1968I.portee: Heman embodies the musical ministry in service of divine worship, showing that liturgical praise requires skill, training, and dedication. His example suggests that in the assembly of God, artistic and musical talents are a legitimate expression of worship, not mere entertainment. That this musician also became a composer invites us to see him as a figure whose entire life—family, professional, artistic—centers around the glory of God.

sens: unit of capacity for liquids, equivalent to about 6 liters
vessel or container holding this amount of liquid
H1969.detail:
1. The hin is a measure of volume used in the Old Testament to evaluate liquids, particularly oil and wine. It is equivalent to about 6 liters (or nearly 5 to 6 pints in old measurements). It is consistently found in the prescriptions of worship, where exact quantities are very important: for example, Exodus 29:40 prescribes "a quarter of a hin of oil" to accompany a grain offering.
2. The word can also refer to the container itself that holds this measure of liquid—the graduated vase or pot used to pour and measure oil or wine during sacrifices and libations.
H1969.origine: The word "hin" comes from ancient Hebrew and designates a standardized measure from the Semitic world. Its exact etymology remains debated, but it is a term attested in other ancient Near Eastern languages, indicating its roots in the commercial and religious practices of the peoples of that region. The measure itself reflects the Israelites' concern for precision in sacrificial worship.
H1969.emploi: The hin appears 19 times in the Old Testament, primarily in the legislative books (Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers) and prophetic books (Ezekiel). It is used almost exclusively to prescribe the quantities of oil and wine intended for sacrifices and libations. Exodus 29:40 and Leviticus 23:13 use it to measure oil and wine offered with lambs; Numbers 15 and 28 mention it for the libations accompanying burnt offerings; Ezekiel 45-46 refers to it in the restored visions of the future temple. It is a technical measure of worship, never used to designate anything else.
H1969.portee: The hin reminds us that Israel's worship was not a vague or sentimental affair, but required precision and respect for divine prescriptions. These exact measures teach that worship must be orderly and faithful to God's commandments. For today's believer, this invites seriousness in prayer and the offering of the heart, without negligence or approximation.

sens: To harm someone by treating them unjustly or cruelly
To overwhelm someone with repeated words or actions
H1970.detail:
1. The verb literally means "to treat someone unjustly or harmfully." It is to cause harm or damage to a person through actions or words. In Job 19:3, Job accuses his friends of morally damaging him by constantly criticizing him: "You have insulted me ten times." 
2. More broadly, the word denotes the action of overwhelming or troubling someone through repeated assaults, as if one were striking them again and again. When Job says, "you have stunned me like this," he expresses that these violent, repeated criticisms have exhausted and deeply hurt him. It is less a physical stupor than an accumulation of moral blows.
H1970.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that expresses the idea of committing an injustice or a reprehensible act. The form used here is the intensive form (Hiphil), which reinforces the idea: one does not merely harm once, but actively and repeatedly. The root evokes the image of striking or treating brutally.
H1970.emploi: This verb appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Job 19:3. Job addresses his three friends (Eliphaz, Bildad, and Zophar) who, thinking they are doing well, reproach him for his misfortunes and press him to repent. Job feels these incessant criticisms as blows that stun him. The context of the book of Job shows that this word describes the harm done to someone not through physical violence, but through repeated words and judgments.
H1970.portee: This word invites us to reflect on the destructive power of our words, especially when they are repeated or spoken without compassion. Job teaches us that criticizing someone without seeking to understand their suffering can stun and overwhelm them. We learn to recognize when our goodwill becomes injustice and to respect the dignity of those who suffer.

sens: The visible appearance of a person, their facial expression
The impression one receives when looking at someone
The external manifestation of what is happening inside
H1971.detail: 1. The word literally designates what one sees when looking at a person's face — their expression, their demeanor, the impression they give off. In Isaiah 3:9, the prophet says that the aspect of the faces of the inhabitants of Jerusalem "testifies against them": their very expression, their countenance, denounces their guilt and pride — they do not even appear ashamed. 2. This aspect is revealing: it involuntarily expresses the inner state, character, and hidden intentions. Here, people shamelessly display their criminality; their faces cry it out. That is why the prophet appeals to this silent witness — the face speaks, it accuses.
H1971.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that means "to see" or "to look" (כָּרָה, karah); it primarily designates the result of this action — what one perceives, what is shown to the eyes. The basic idea is that of a "visible appearance," what is presented to the gaze and reveals something about the person.
H1971.emploi: This word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Isaiah 3:9. The prophet uses it to accuse the inhabitants of Jerusalem: their faces, by their very expression, denounce their iniquity. They resemble the Sodomites who were not afraid to publicly proclaim their sins. The word summarizes the idea that the evil of which one is not ashamed eventually becomes inscribed on one's features — one becomes what one does.
H1971.portee: This verse reminds us that it is difficult to hide for long what we truly are. The expression of our face, our attitude, our way of being betray our deep convictions and our relationship with God. For the believer, it is an invitation to let the peace and grace of Christ transform not only their heart but also their face — to not be afraid to openly show their faith rather than live in shame and concealment.

sens: To be pushed away, forcibly removed
To be expelled from a place or community
To be scattered, put to flight
(Figuratively) To be rejected, excluded
H1972.detail:
1. The word describes the action of being pushed away or removed violently, like someone being chased away. It is a forced separation imposed on the victim: in Micah 4:7, those who had been "chased away" — scattered, exiled — will be restored by God and will form a powerful nation.
2. It evokes expulsion from a place: being put outside, rejected, forced to leave against one's will.
3. More broadly, the verb can describe the fleeing or scattering of an entire group, particularly in the context of exile or persecution.
4. Figuratively, it can mean being morally or spiritually rejected, being set apart from the community of the covenant.
H1972.origine: The Hebrew verb הלא (halak in its simple root) fundamentally means "to go" or "to move," but in the Niphal form — the passive form — it takes on the meaning of "to be chased away" or "to be removed far away." The preposition "far away" reinforces the idea of forced distance. This passive form shows that the subject undergoes the action without being able to control it: they are not active, but passive, a victim of the removal.
H1972.emploi: This verb appears only once in the consulted Segond translations, in Micah 4:7. It is used to describe the fate of the lame and the weak — those who had been "chased away," that is, scattered or exiled — to whom God promises to restore power and unity. The context is that of a messianic restoration: from scattered victims, they will become a strong nation. The word fits into the prophetic theme of the reversal of the fate of the oppressed.
H1972.portee: This passage speaks of hope for those who feel excluded or scattered. God sees those who have been "chased away" — the marginalized, the exiled, the weak — and He promises to transform them into a powerful nation. For the believer, this affirms that God does not abandon those who suffer from rejection or separation, and that present humiliation may be the prelude to future exaltation under the reign of the Messiah.

sens: Beyond a place, further in space
After a moment, in the future or later
Existence, continuity in time
H1973.detail:
1. The word primarily evokes a direction or distance: a place located further away, beyond where one is. When Samuel says to Saul "you will go further," he indicates a path to continue (1 Samuel 10:3). It also conveys the idea of exceeding a limit: the arrows fall "beyond" the one who receives them (1 Samuel 20:22).
2. The word also applies to the time that comes: the "following" days of an offering (Leviticus 22:27), or the future of a nation. It is the movement towards what is not yet, like a road that extends into tomorrow.
3. Finally, the word can express existence or persistence: a nation that "exists" and continues to be what it is (Isaiah 18:2). It conveys the idea of lasting, remaining in place or in effect.
H1973.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root that means "to go beyond" or "to exceed." Its starting image is that of movement: one goes further, one advances. It naturally extends to time (continuing into the future) and to existence (persisting, enduring). The word belongs to the family of adverbs of direction and time in Hebrew.
H1973.emploi: This word appears 16 times in the Hebrew Bible, mainly in historical narratives and the prophets. It primarily describes movements in space: "move away far" says to Lot, or "the arrows are beyond you" to David. It also applies to the succession of time: the days that follow an offering. Sometimes it carries the idea of persistence or a lasting reality: a nation that "exists" and subsists. Its meaning varies according to context, but the central idea remains that of what exceeds a given point — in space, time, or being.
H1973.portee: This word speaks of progression, movement forward, and the trust that must be placed in God to advance. When it comes to distance, it reminds us that God always sends us "further" than our present knowledge. When it comes to time, it invites us to align our steps with the rhythm of His will, not our impatience. It is a word for those who hesitate to follow God beyond known paths.

sens: State of joy and shared happiness
Festivity, joyful celebration with feast and entertainment
Praise expressed through joy and celebration
H1974.detail:
1. Rejoicing is primarily an inner state of intense joy. In Leviticus 19:24, the fruits of the fourth year are "consecrated to the Lord amidst rejoicing": it is the joy that accompanies a religious act and a recognized blessing.

2. This word also designates the feast itself, the moment when people celebrate together. In Judges 9:27, the grape harvesters "engaged in rejoicing" — they ate, drank, and entertained themselves together after the harvest, which shows how rejoicing is a collective action, a feast with food and drink.

3. Through its religious context, rejoicing becomes a form of praise: it is through shared joy and celebration that we honor God and recognize His gifts. The feast is not merely entertainment, but a way to celebrate with gratitude.
H1974.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root expressing the idea of a cry, a joyful proclamation. It primarily denotes the audible and visible expression of joy — hence its constant link with feasts, banquets, and collective festivities. It is a word that paints uncontained joy, one that manifests through cries, music, and sharing.
H1974.emploi: The word appears only twice in the Hebrew Bible. Both usages are similar: Leviticus 19:24 uses it in a religious and agricultural context (the fruits offered to the Lord in joy), while Judges 9:27 shows it in a context of pagan celebration, where rejoicing accompanies worship (eating, drinking, and cursing Abimelech). In both cases, it is a collective feast that creates an atmosphere of shared joy and expresses either gratitude towards God or the celebration of the divine according to the beliefs of the time.
H1974.portee: This word reminds us that joy and celebration are not shameful in God's eyes — they are part of the believing life when rooted in gratitude and devotion. It also invites us to see that our joy can be first shared, collective, a joy that unites believers and expresses gratitude together.

sens: that which is close to the speaker or has just been mentioned
this one, this particular person or thing
this, that (demonstrative adjective)
that one, in the sense of a person or thing distant or already named
H1975.detail:
1. The word designates something specific that is near or has just been said — it is a demonstrative that shows and designates. In Judges 6:20, the angel says to Gideon: place the food on "this" rock, meaning the rock that is there, in front of him, visible and precise.
2. It can mean "this one" or "this one" when it replaces a noun or specifies it: in 1 Samuel 17:26, David speaks of the Philistine at that moment, "this" Philistine, the one just mentioned — it is a demonstrative of proximity.
3. It also simply serves as an adjective to show a person or thing: in 2 Kings 4:25, Elisha cries out "Here is this Shunammite!" — the word points to the woman he sees coming.
4. In certain contexts, it can evoke "that one" or "that other," marking a certain distance or distinction: in 1 Samuel 14:1, Jonathan speaks of the Philistine outpost "that is over there on the other side."
H1975.origine: It is a Hebrew demonstrative of the type "ha-" (the) reinforced by an element marking proximity or designation. The form derives from roots meaning "to show" or "to designate" — it is in the same family as other Hebrew demonstratives and appears already in the oldest biblical texts. It is a structural word, intended to point out and distinguish named realities in the narrative.
H1975.emploi: This word appears 7 times in the provided Hebrew Bible. It is always a demonstrative: sometimes an adjective ("this rock", "this Philistine"), sometimes a pronoun ("this one"). It is found in the historical books — Judges, 1 Samuel, 2 Kings — and also in prophetic visions like Daniel. In 1 Samuel 14:1, it marks a direction or locality ("the other side"). In 2 Kings 23:17, it points to a monument that is seen. In each case, it anchors the narrative in the immediate: what is seen, what has just been said, what is there.
H1975.portee: This word reminds us that the Bible is a narrative made up of concrete and visible things. It immerses us in the scene — we see this rock, we hear about this Philistine, we catch sight of this woman approaching. It is the mark of a God who acts in particular and named history, not in the abstract. By reading these demonstratives, we enter into the real time and space of living faith.

sens: Pronoun of direct designation or proximity: this one, that one, etc.
Interrogative pronoun: who is this man or person?
H1976.detail: 1. The word expresses a designation or identification: it points to someone or something specific, often with a nuance of proximity or distinction. In Genesis 37:19, the brothers see Joseph approaching and say, "Here comes the dreamer who arrives" — "who" designates Joseph precisely and sometimes slightly distantly. 2. It can also serve to formulate a question of identification: "Who is this man?" Rebecca asks in Genesis 24:65. She designates someone she sees but does not recognize, and seeks to know who he is.
H1976.origine: A fundamental Hebrew word of designation and identification, built on the idea of pointing to a present or visible reality. The form with the article "ha-" ("the") reinforces the sense of proximity or clarity: "this one, that one." It belongs to the family of Hebrew demonstratives, essential tools for narration and identification in the biblical text.
H1976.emploi: This word appears twice in the provided usages, both in Genesis. In Genesis 24:65, Rebecca sees a man in the fields and asks the servant, "Who is this man?" — the pronoun functions as an interrogative of identification. In Genesis 37:19, the brothers see Joseph from afar and say, "Here comes the dreamer who arrives" — here the pronoun designates someone specific, with a hint of mockery or disdain. In both cases, the word serves to identify or question the identity of a person in a narrative scene.
H1976.portee: This small word reminds us that the Bible speaks of concrete individuals, of faces, of real encounters. When Rebecca asks, "Who is this man?", she shows us a person who does not yet know she will experience a love story; when the brothers recognize Joseph as "the dreamer", they reveal their envy and hostility. These moments of identification mark turning points: the Bible loves to show how one recognizes someone, and what that changes.

sens: This, that thing or person being talked about
That one, that (to indicate something far away or in time)
H1977.detail:
1. It is a word that shows and designates: it points to someone or something specific, often close to the speaker. In Ezekiel 36:35, when the prophet says "this devastated land," he is not speaking vaguely: he is designating the land of Israel in particular, the one his listeners know, the one he brings to their minds. The word creates a sense of closeness, an immediacy.
2. But it can also refer to something distant in space or time — something seen "over there" or recalled from memory. It is a gesture of the hand: "that one, this one." The demonstrative establishes both distance and clarity at the same time: it is this one, not another.
H1977.origine: It is a fundamental Hebrew demonstrative, formed from a root that expresses the idea of showing and distinguishing. In Hebrew, demonstratives serve to designate concrete things and make them present to the listener's mind — much more strongly than in our modern languages. This word belongs to the same family as other Hebrew demonstratives, all constructed to create this sensation of showing: "There it is!" It is one of the tools of poetic and prophetic language to make things vivid and visible.
H1977.emploi: This word appears only once in the provided biblical usages: in Ezekiel 36:35, where the prophet speaks of a land that will be transformed. Ezekiel thus designates the land of Israel with particular force: not just "any" land, but "this" land, that of the promise, the one his contemporaries know as devastated and ruined. Through this demonstrative, the prophet makes hope concrete and present: he does not prophesy in the abstract, he shows and affirms. The choice of this word is not neutral — it is an act of faith that designates what will be, as if it were already there.
H1977.portee: This small word teaches us that prophetic speech is never vague: it shows, it designates, it makes God's promise present and concrete. When Ezekiel says "this land," he is not describing a concept; he is affirming that God will transform, here and now (or soon), the real place where his listeners live. For the reader, this demonstrative reminds us that Christian hope does not float in the clouds: it looks at the world as it is and proclaims that God acts in it, that He restores, that He makes fruitful. "This will happen."

sens: The lower part of the leg, from the knee to the tips of the toes
What allows one to walk, to move
The place where one places the foot, the ground
What supports, that on which something rests
The imprint or trace of a person
H1978.detail: 1. The foot is literally the part of the body at the bottom of the leg, where we place our toes when we walk: in Job 29:6, the feet of the righteous bathe in cream, an image of prosperity and abundance. 2. By extension, the word also refers to the very action of walking or moving from one place to another. 3. It can evoke the ground, the terrain on which one relies to advance. 4. Sometimes, the foot symbolizes what supports, what provides a stable base for something. 5. It can also refer to the visible imprint left by the foot when walking: the trace of a person.
H1978.origine: The Hebrew word ha-likh comes from a root that means "to walk" or "to go." The foot, in Semitic languages, is closely related to the idea of movement and displacement: it is by the feet that one walks. This word is related to other Hebrew terms that denote walking and the path.
H1978.emploi: This word appears only once in the Bible: in Job 29:6, where the patriarch Job enumerates the wealth and blessing he enjoyed before his misfortunes. The image of feet bathing in cream expresses superabundance, extreme prosperity, a life where everything is comfort and opulence. This poetic and figurative context shows how the foot, a symbol of the living being and its action, also becomes the symbol of one who enjoys goods.
H1978.portee: This image of the foot bathed in cream reminds us that prosperity in the Bible is often described in concrete and sensual terms: these are not abstractions, but realities that the whole body experiences. For Job, God's blessing affects the whole person, from foot to head. It is also a reminder that the sufferer has known better days, which makes his fall all the more tragic and evokes compassion.

sens: The action of going on foot, moving from one place to another
Group of travelers on the move, caravan
Manner of walking, pace, movement of the body in action
Conduct, way of behaving or acting
Path, road, trail traveled
H1979.detail:
1. Walking is primarily the physical action of advancing on foot: in Psalms 68:25, we behold "the walk" of God, meaning His coming, His majestic movement in the sanctuary.
2. The word also refers to a group of people traveling together: in Job 6:19, the "travelers" (literally the caravans) of Tema and Sheba traverse the deserts, forming convoys of merchants or pilgrims.
3. Walking can evoke the particular way of moving: in Nahum 2:6, the valiant warriors "stumble in their walk," losing their assurance and vigor.
4. The word broadens to mean conduct or behavior: in Proverbs 31:27, "what happens" in the house is literally the walk, meaning the management and unfolding of domestic affairs.
5. By extension, walking becomes the path itself: in Habakkuk 3:6, "the ancient paths" open before God, meaning the old roads that the Lord traverses in His coming.
H1979.origine: The word comes from the Hebrew root that means "to go, to walk." It is linked to the fundamental image of movement and displacement in space, very present in Hebrew thought to describe both physical action and the conduct or destiny of a person. The same root produces words to denote the way, the step, and the gait.
H1979.emploi: This word appears five times in the Hebrew Bible, primarily in poetic texts (Psalms, Proverbs, Nahum, Habakkuk) and in Job. Its concrete meaning of "walking, moving" dominates when it comes to travelers or characters in action. But the Bible also imbues it with figurative meanings: the walk of God evokes His active presence and sovereign power; the walk of a person or a household symbolizes their conduct, their affairs, their governance. The poetic context enriches the word with spiritual nuances.
H1979.portee: This word reminds the reader that walking is never trivial: God's walk manifests His majesty and authority; that of men reveals their inner state, their courage or weakness, and engages their responsibility. To contemplate or keep watch over the paths is to keep watch over one's own conduct and that of one's household. Walking is a powerful biblical image of the Christian life itself.

sens: to move from one place to another, by foot or otherwise
to leave, depart from a place
to come, arrive
to advance, progress in time or direction
to lead one's life, conduct oneself (figuratively)
to die (figuratively)
H1980G.detail:
1. To move from one place to another: the most common and concrete meaning of the verb. It is used for any movement, whether on foot or not. In Genesis 3:14, the serpent "will go" on its belly, meaning it will move by crawling.
2. To leave, depart from a place, to distance oneself: the emphasis is on the point of departure and the act of distancing. Abraham "goes" to Canaan in Genesis 12:1-4, he leaves his country.
3. To come, arrive: the same verb also denotes arrival or approach. In Judges 19:17, the old man asks the traveler: "Where are you going, and where are you coming from?" (the same word for going and coming).
4. To advance, progress: in time or according to a given direction, surpassing a stage. Tamar "went" to Amnon's house in 2 Samuel 13:8 to accomplish a specific action.
5. To lead one's life, conduct oneself: in a figurative sense, it refers to the manner of living or behaving. God "walks" before Israel in Numbers 14:14, meaning He guides and leads them.
6. To die: a rare figurative usage, where "to go" means to leave life, to pass from life to death.
H1980G.origine: The Hebrew verb halakh comes from a root that evokes the idea of movement and passage. It has several forms in Hebrew: the simple form (Qal) for "to go, to walk," the intensive form (Piel) for "to walk, to traverse," the reflexive form (Hithpael) for "to stroll, to move back and forth," and the passive form (Niphal) for "to be led, to be guided." It is one of the most frequent verbs in the Hebrew Bible.
H1980G.emploi: This verb is extremely common in biblical Hebrew: over 830 occurrences in the Old Testament. It appears in all books and carries various nuances depending on the context. In its literal sense, it describes the movements of characters: Abraham going to Canaan (Genesis 12), Jacob fleeing to Laban (Genesis 28), Abraham's servants going to find a wife (Genesis 24). In its figurative sense, it expresses moral or spiritual conduct: "to walk" before God (to live piously), "to go" after other gods (idolatry). The verb sometimes shifts in nuance: in a sentence, "to go" and "to come" use the same root to denote movement from the speaker's perspective.
H1980G.portee: For the Christian reader, this verb is fundamental: it speaks of the movement of human existence before God. "Going" towards the Lord signifies obedience and the pilgrimage of faith. Conversely, "going" far from God or "after" idols describes sin and waywardness. The word invites reflection on the direction of one's life: to whom and to what am I heading? It is a verb of journey and decision.

sens: To move from one place to another, by foot or on the way
To arrive somewhere, to present oneself before someone
To set out, undertake a journey
To progress, advance in a direction or project
To conduct one's life in a certain way, to live
H1980H.detail:
1. To move on foot or on the way from one place to another. The word describes the simplest physical movement: to walk, to travel. Jacob sets out and "went" to the land of the sons of the East (Genesis 29:1).

2. To arrive at a destination, to present oneself before someone or approach a place. This is the culmination of the journey: Balaam receives a messenger who "comes" to tell him that Balak is calling him (Numbers 22:16).

3. To leave a place, to go away. This is the point of departure: the prophet is warned not to take the path he "went" back (1 Kings 13:17).

4. To go somewhere in a crowd, to flock. Peoples will "go" to the mountain of the Lord to receive His teaching (Isaiah 2:3).

5. To advance, progress in a direction or toward a goal: the expression "to go after" someone means to follow or obey them, to lead one's life in a certain direction.

6. To live, to lead one's existence in a certain way. In a figurative sense, "to go" describes how one traverses life, particularly in wisdom literature: how someone "walks" morally.
H1980H.origine: The Hebrew verb halakh is a fundamental word of movement and path. It shares its root with the noun halakh ("path"), which evokes the traveled route. The verb exists in several forms: the simple form (Qal) for the direct action "to go" or "to walk," the intensive form (Piel) for repeated or deliberate walking, and other forms that mark nuances and variations. In biblical usage, the verb quickly enriches itself with figurative meanings: one "walks" in the ways of God, one "goes" after idols, one "goes" to death. It is a deeply existential word: halakh speaks of the road one takes, thus of choices and destiny.
H1980H.emploi: This verb has 43 occurrences in the provided corpus and dominates the entire Old Testament. It appears in all books, from narratives (Genesis, Judges, Samuel, Kings) to wisdom literature (Job, Proverbs) and the prophets (Isaiah, Jeremiah, Micah). In its concrete sense, it denotes physical movement: Jacob "goes" eastward, a messenger "comes" to Saul, peoples "go" to the temple. In its moral and spiritual sense, its importance increases: one "walks" with God, one "goes" after other gods, one "walks" in the paths of the Lord. The verses in Isaiah 2:3 and Micah 4:2 highlight a prophetic usage where nations "will go" to Mount Zion to learn the eternal ways. Thus, it is a verb of biblical realism: it speaks of both the earthly road and the spiritual path.
H1980H.portee: This verb invites the reader to meditate on the direction and meaning of their life. In the Bible, "to go" is never neutral: it is always going somewhere, or toward someone, or according to a will. Asking "where are you going?" is akin to asking "who are you following?" and "how are you living?" The word teaches that the Christian faith is not a static state, but a journey: one walks with God, follows Him, and progresses. This sheds light on Christ's call to His disciples: "Follow me," which is an invitation to set out, to go where He goes.

sens: To move on foot from one place to another, to make a journey
To move, go, circulate (for a river, an animal, a person)
To follow a path, a direction, to adopt a way of life
To live according to a rule, commandments, or an example (in a figurative sense)
To progress, advance in time or in a situation
To accompany someone, to be with them in a relationship
H1980I.detail:
1. The primary and concrete meaning: to move on foot over a distance. In Joshua 18:4, three men are sent to "explore" the land and draw up a plan. It is the physical action of moving from one place to another.
2. To extend, circulate, to flow: the river Hiddekel "flows" (Genesis 2:14), meaning it moves, traverses space. The word describes all progressive movement.
3. To adopt a conduct, to follow a moral path: in 2 Kings 8:18, the king "walked in the way of the kings of Israel" — he imitated their behavior. In Psalms 1:1, not to "walk according to the counsel of the wicked" means not to adopt their principles.
4. To obey a law, to live according to rules: in Jeremiah 44:10, the people did not "follow" the law of God. In Leviticus 26:3, to walk in the statutes of the Lord means to respect them, to make them one's way of life.
5. To advance in a relationship with God: Enoch "walked with God" (Genesis 5:24), an intimate and lasting communion, a progression in divine intimacy.
6. To be led, guided: in Exodus 13:21, the Lord "went" before Israel in the form of a pillar — He accompanied, guided, and bore the people.
H1980I.origine: The Hebrew verb halakh (הָלַךְ) is one of the most fundamental movement verbs. Its root expresses the simple idea of moving, going from one point to another. The word has generated various forms (simple, intensive, causative) that amplify or modulate this meaning: to walk, to make walk, to walk together. In the Hebrew Bible, this verb is very frequent (over 1500 occurrences) and quickly becomes a key word for speaking about the way of life, moral and spiritual conduct — a natural image of life as a path that one travels.
H1980I.emploi: This verb is one of the most commonly used in the Hebrew Bible, appearing 305 times in the books of the Old Testament in translations like the Segond. It first appears in the literal sense: men walk, animals walk, rivers flow. Very quickly, it takes on figurative and spiritual meanings: to walk becomes to follow a law, to adopt a conduct. It is massively encountered in the Torah (Genesis, Exodus, Leviticus, Deuteronomy), where it designates the behavior of the people towards God, obedience or disobedience (Leviticus 26 is a striking example, with repetitions of "walk"). It also enriches the Psalms and Proverbs (Psalms 1:1: not to walk according to the counsel of the wicked) where it describes the two paths: that of wisdom and that of folly. The expression "walk with God" (Genesis 5:24 with Enoch) becomes a model of intimacy and spiritual communion.
H1980I.portee: This word teaches the reader that the spiritual life is a walk, a path to be traveled. Every choice, every day, we "walk" in a direction: that of God or that of the world. This emphasizes concrete obedience and personal responsibility — faith is not just a static belief, but a conduct, a commitment to follow. Meditating on the image of the path also invites perseverance and communion: we progress with God, like Enoch, or we drift away from Him. It is a call to be attentive to the direction of one's life.

sens: To go, walk, move from one place to another
To lead someone with oneself, to take them away
To guide someone on a path, to direct them
To carry something away
To live in a certain way, to lead a certain life
H1980J.detail:
1. The simplest meaning: to move on foot from one place to another. It is the basic movement, as when one says "go, come, walk." Deuteronomy 8:2 refers to the forty years of walking in the desert, during which God led His people.

2. To take someone with oneself, to forcibly take them or take responsibility for them. It is to take someone by the hand or by command and make them move forward. In 2 Chronicles 33:11, the Assyrians led Manasseh into captivity in Babylon; in Jeremiah 32:5, the king of Babylon will take Zedekiah away.

3. To guide someone on a path they do not know, to orient them, to protect them by leading them. It is the image of the shepherd guiding his flock. Isaiah 42:16 speaks of God leading the blind along paths they do not know; Psalms 106:9 recounts how God made them walk through the sea.

4. To carry something, to transport it from one place to another. In Exodus 2:9, the child Moses is taken away.

5. To live, to lead a life, to adopt a certain way of conducting oneself (figurative sense). The word then describes the general direction of existence, as in Proverbs 16:29 where someone leads their neighbor on a bad path.
H1980J.origine: This Hebrew verb is very ancient and very common. It comes from a root that means to walk, to advance. The word belongs to a broad family: it is found in nouns (like "path"). The basic image is that of the body's movement progressing, step by step, from one point to another. It is a concrete verb, rooted in the bodily experience of the nomadic and pastoral people of Israel.
H1980J.emploi: This verb is one of the most frequent in the Hebrew Bible (36 occurrences in the Segond). It appears in all books, from historical narrative to Psalms, from the Law to the Prophets. Its basic meaning "to go, to walk" is constant, but the Bible enriches it: God "leads" His people in the desert, kings "take" prisoners into captivity, enemies "make" their victims walk. The verb changes nuance depending on who acts (God who guides, a king who commands, an enemy who forces) and depending on the object (a person, a path, an entire life). In Hebrew grammatical forms, the meaning can emphasize the simple action (to go) or the causative action (to make go, to lead).
H1980J.portee: This verb invites the believer to meditate on the notion of direction and guidance. When the Bible says that God "leads," it assures us that we are not left to chance: we are taken care of, oriented, protected. But the verb also challenges us: we are responsible for the path we take and for the one we lead others towards. Living is not drifting; it is walking — and it is deciding where to walk.

sens: To move from one place to another, to walk
To move, to set out, to leave
To come towards someone, to approach
To die, to disappear (figurative sense)
To live, to lead a life (figurative sense)
To traverse, to cover a space
H1980K.detail:
1. The most common meaning: to physically move from one place to another. In Genesis 37:13, the father says to Joseph, "Go see your brothers"; this simply asks him to move to find them.
2. To set out, to leave, to depart from a place. When Nehemiah says (Nehemiah 2:17), "Come and let us build," he calls the people to rise and take action.
3. To come, to approach someone. Lot's daughters say (Genesis 19:32), "Come, let us make our father drink wine": they invite him to join them.
4. To die, to cease living (used as a euphemism). When someone is said to have "gone away," it can mean they have passed away.
5. To live, to conduct one's existence in a certain way. Psalm 34:12 asks, "Who is the man who desires life?" — meaning one who wants to live well.
6. To traverse, to cover a territory or distance. The verb can express the idea of covering a space, of walking through.
H1980K.origine: A very ancient root in Hebrew, halakh fundamentally means "to move, to advance." It evokes the concrete image of a person or creature putting one foot in front of the other. It is one of the most basic and commonly used verbs in the Hebrew language. It generates several grammatical forms that nuance the meaning: a simple form ("I go"), an intensive form ("he walks, strolls"), a passive form ("he is led"). In the Greek version of the Old Testament, it is often translated as poreuomai (πορεύομαι), which also carries the idea of walking and movement.
H1980K.emploi: This verb appears about 51 times in the provided texts, especially in historical narratives and biblical poems. It is very frequent in Genesis and in the historical books (Samuel, Kings), where it describes concrete movements: going to see someone, going to war, going somewhere. In the Psalms and Isaiah, it takes on more figurative nuances: "come, let us worship" (Psalm 95:1), "let us go to the house of the Lord" (Isaiah 2:3). The grammatical forms vary: as an imperative, it is a direct call ("Go! Come!"), very common in commands and invitations; in simple narrative, it describes a completed action; in poetic parallelism, it expresses moral or spiritual movement.
H1980K.portee: This verb reminds us that the Christian faith is a journey, a walk. God calls His children not to remain still but to advance, to set out towards Him and according to His will. "Come" is also the ultimate call: a personal, warm invitation that implies a relationship. Meditating on this verb prompts us to ask: where am I going? Who is calling me? Am I moving towards God?

sens: To move from one place to another on foot or in motion
To progress, to extend, to develop
To continue, to persevere in an action or state
To die, to live (figurative sense of going through life)
To advance in a given direction
To be in the process of realization
H1980L.detail:
1. The fundamental meaning is physical movement: to move from one place to another. In Genesis 8:3, after the Flood, the waters "went away" — they gradually receded from the ground. It is the simple idea of moving, walking, departing.

2. Very often, the word denotes progression, continuous growth. In 2 Samuel 5:10, David "became greater and greater": the verb "go" conveys the idea that something is advancing, amplifying, gradually growing. Similarly, in 1 Samuel 2:26, Samuel "grew" in favor.

3. The verb also expresses continuity, perseverance — one "goes forward" in a path or situation. When Proverbs 4:18 speaks of the path of the righteous that "shines ever brighter," it is the image of a continuous walk towards the light.

4. In a figurative sense, "go" can mean to live, to go through life, and even to die. In Genesis 15:2, Abraham says, "I am going away childless": the image is that of a traveler continuing his journey towards the end of his life.

5. The word also describes a directional advance in space or an action. In Joshua 8:13, Joshua "advanced" in the valley — he moved towards the military objective.
H1980L.origine: The Hebrew verb הָלַךְ (halakh) comes from a root expressing physical movement. It is a very ancient word, probably of common Semitic origin. The root primarily evokes the concrete idea of walking, from which images of progression, continuity, and even life journeys emerge. Nouns from the same family designate paths or ways of living.
H1980L.emploi: The verb "go" is one of the most frequent in the Old Testament, used 34 times in these excerpts. It takes on various grammatical forms that nuance its meaning: the Qal (simple form) expresses movement or progression; the Piel adds the idea of repeated or continued walking; the Hithpael (reflexive form) reinforces the idea of crossing or traversing; the Niphal (passive form) often expresses the idea of being led or guided. In the narratives of Genesis and Joshua, "go" describes concrete movements (Abraham traveling, Joshua advancing into battle). In the Psalms and Proverbs, the word becomes more abstract: it speaks of growing, progressing morally or spiritually. In 2 Samuel and 1 Chronicles, it emphasizes the gradual growth of a power or divine favor.
H1980L.portee: This verb reminds us that the believer's life is a continuous movement towards God. Like David who "grew greater and greater" with the Lord's help (2 Samuel 5:10), the Christian is called to advance in faith, to progress continually. This word invites us not to remain static, but to "walk" day after day in obedience and trust, remembering that God Himself directs our path.

sens: to move from one place to another, to walk
to leave a place, to depart
to travel, to go on a journey
to die, to end one's life
to conduct oneself, to live in a certain way
to lead, to cause to advance
H1980M.detail:
1. The primary meaning is simply to move physically: to walk, to go from one point to another. Abram watches the victors leave after the battle (Genesis 14:11), or Rebekah gets on a camel to go to Isaac (Genesis 24:61). It is the concrete movement of the body from one place to another.
2. To depart means to leave a specific place to go elsewhere. When the Lord "went away" after speaking to Abraham, He leaves His presence (Genesis 18:33). The servant also "departs" with Rebekah: he begins the journey back.
3. Route or path evokes the sense of the journey itself, the idea of covering a distance. Esau suggests to Jacob: "Let us go, let us set out" (Genesis 33:12), meaning: let us begin the journey, let us take the path.
4. To die or "to go away" in the sense of leaving life—the verb can figuratively evoke death, as a form of definitive departure, since living is also to "go" from one day to the next.
5. To conduct oneself, to live in a certain way: the verb can refer to how one traverses life, one's habitual behavior. It is the figurative use of movement: how one "walks" morally or spiritually.
6. To lead, to cause someone to advance: the servant "takes" Rebekah, he makes her go with him. Here the verb expresses the action of leading someone to a place.
H1980M.origine: A very common Hebrew root that expresses fundamental movement: to go, to walk. It is rooted in the image of the leg moving forward, of the body that moves. The verb can be used in the simple form (one says "he goes"), in the frequentative form ("he usually walks"), or in the causative form ("he causes to go"). This root is one of the most productive in Hebrew, used as early as Genesis for all human or divine movements.
H1980M.emploi: This verb appears 11 times in the provided usages, mainly in Genesis where it describes the movements of the patriarchs: Abraham, Lot, Rebekah, Jacob, Esau. The usage is very concrete and narrative: it recounts who goes where and when. It can also describe divine movements (the Lord "goes away"), suggesting that God moves like men, while having His sovereignty. In Ecclesiastes, it evokes the weariness of one who must go without wisdom (Ecclesiastes 10:15). In Daniel, the eschatological context of the verb "go" refers to the movement of future events (Daniel 12:9). The verb thus adapts from the concrete of travel to the figurative of conduct and existence.
H1980M.portee: For the believer, this verb reminds us that life is a movement, a path to be traveled. Being a Christian also means to "go" somewhere, to advance in faith. The verb can encourage one to leave sin (to go away from temptation), to depart where God calls, or to walk in a certain moral direction. It is also a humble verb: the patriarchs "go" simply, without pretense, for to go is also to recognize that one has not yet arrived, that one is on the way to a promise.

sens: To move from one place to another, to walk, to move
To depart, to leave a place
To follow someone, to go behind them
To conduct oneself in a certain way, to adopt a line of conduct
To serve, to obey, to follow the ways of someone
To go in pursuit of something, to seek
H1980N.detail:
1. To move from one place to another: this is the simplest meaning, that of physical walking. "Led by their counsel, he went with Joram" (2 Chronicles 22:5): Ahaziah goes to Joram for a military campaign. It is a concrete movement in space.

2. To depart, to leave a place: the word also denotes the action of distancing oneself, of leaving a place. "Should I take your son to the land from which you came?" (Genesis 24:5) implies Abraham's departure to a new land.

3. To follow someone: "to go after" means to be behind, to place oneself under the direction of a person. "You have not sought young men" (Ruth 3:10): Boaz praises Ruth for not having run after the young men of the village.

4. To conduct oneself, to adopt a line of conduct: the verb also describes the manner of living. "You have walked after me with all your heart" (1 Kings 14:8): David followed the commandments of the Lord, meaning he obeyed and conducted himself according to divine will.

5. To serve, to obey, to follow the ways: this is the most theological usage. "If you do not go after other gods" (Jeremiah 7:6): do not serve other gods, do not turn to them and obey them.

6. To go in pursuit, to seek: the word can also mean to actively search, to run after. This is a nuance of the previous meaning, but directed towards quest or desire.
H1980N.origine: The Hebrew verb halakh comes from a root that evokes the movement of feet, walking. Its root is present in several words of the same family related to path and progression. In Hebrew, this verb is one of the most common to express movement, first physical, then figurative (moral or religious conduct). The figurative sense—walking in the ways of God—becomes central in biblical thought: to believe is to "walk" with the Lord, to follow His direction.
H1980N.emploi: This verb appears about 74 times in the Old Testament, in all historical, prophetic, and poetic books. It first denotes simple physical displacement (to go somewhere, to depart), then quickly takes on a moral and religious dimension. The figurative usage "to go after" (to follow the ways of God or idols) is extremely frequent in the prophets Jeremiah and Hosea: it describes the unfaithfulness of Israel who "goes after other gods." David, on the contrary, "walks after" the Lord (1 Kings 14:8). The verb can also simply describe a daily action: Ruth "goes to the fields" or Boaz "goes to the gate." Its meaning thus progressively enriches: physical walking becomes the image of living morally and religiously.
H1980N.portee: This word reveals a profound truth of biblical faith: that our "walk"—that is, our conduct and obedience—is what defines our relationship with God. To go after God is to follow Him in action, not just in word. Conversely, to go after other gods or idols is to betray the covenant. For the Christian, this verb reminds us that faith is lived out daily, in the direction we choose, as a continual act of following the Lord.

sens: To push back, to drive away, to force aside
To send someone in a direction
To regularly direct, to make go in a habitual manner
H1980O.detail:
1. The primary meaning is physical: to push aside or drive something away with force. When the Lord "pushes back" the sea in Exodus 14:21, the east wind drives the waters back, separates them, and leaves a dry path — an image of divine power mastering nature.
2. The word extends to the idea of sending or leading someone, making them go somewhere. It is to direct a movement.
3. Used in a figurative or habitual sense, it denotes a repeated or regular action: to address "frequently" letters (Nehemiah 6:17) means to send them continuously, to make them go back and forth incessantly.
H1980O.origine: The Hebrew verb halakh (הָלַךְ) expresses fundamental movement: to go, to walk, to come. Its root evokes the movement of the body from one place to another. Depending on the verbal mode used (Qal, Piel, Hithpael, Niphal), it takes on nuances: the simple form means to go, the intensive form (Piel) emphasizes the action of walking or directing, and the causative form (Niphal) stresses the act of being led or leading. It is one of the most frequent verbs in the Hebrew Bible.
H1980O.emploi: This verb appears hundreds of times in biblical Hebrew in all types of contexts. Here, the three uses show its flexibility: it can describe a spectacular natural phenomenon (Exodus 14:21, where the sea is pushed back), an administrative or social action (Nehemiah 6:17, where letters are sent regularly), and an act of forced or voluntary leading (2 Kings 17:27, depending on the context). The meaning varies according to the object of the verb — one pushes back water, sends letters, leads people — but the idea of movement and direction remains central.
H1980O.portee: Meditating on this verb reminds us that God's will moves all things: He pushes back obstacles to open paths for His people, He sends His servants to carry His message, He directs history. Recognizing how the Lord "makes things go" according to His plan invites the believer to trust in divine direction, even when it seems impossible.

sens: To move by putting one foot in front of the other
To walk, to go from one place to another
To advance, to progress in a direction
To conduct oneself, to behave in a certain manner
H1981.detail:
1. The fundamental meaning is that of physical movement: to walk on one's feet, to advance step by step. It is the most concrete image of the verb. In Daniel 3:25, the three young Hebrews "walk" in the fiery furnace — they physically move without being consumed.
2. To walk can also describe a stroll, a leisurely movement in a space: to wander, to roam, or to circulate in a place. Nebuchadnezzar "walked" in his royal palace (Daniel 4:29), showing the idea of locomotion without haste, in a context of leisure or possession.
3. In a figurative sense, to walk expresses the idea of progressing, advancing in a direction or undertaking. It is the movement of progress.
4. The verb finally acquires a moral sense: "to walk" means to conduct oneself, to behave in a certain manner. In Daniel 4:37, those who "walk" with pride are those whose behavior is marked by pride — "to walk" here describes a way of living and acting.
H1981.origine: The Hebrew verb halakh comes from a very ancient root expressing fundamental physical movement. It is one of the most common verbs of displacement in Semitic languages. The language evokes the primary image of the body advancing, and from there gradually detaches an ethical or moral sense: one "walks" in a way, one "walks" according to principles. The same root generates derivatives related to the path and walking, from the most concrete to the most abstract.
H1981.emploi: This verb appears 3 times in the provided uses, all drawn from the book of Daniel, which dates from the late period. In Daniel 3:25, it describes an act of impossible physical locomotion (walking in the fire without burning) — it is a miracle. In Daniel 4:29, it evokes the daily stroll of a king, a free walk in his domain. In Daniel 4:37, the verb becomes moral: to walk with pride means to conduct oneself with arrogance. The word thus applies to very different contexts, from the marvelous to ethical behavior, depending on the narrative context.
H1981.portee: This verb invites the reader to meditate on the relationship between physical movement and moral conduct. The Bible never completely separates body and soul: "to walk" as a creature made of flesh also says something about our spiritual walk. Those who walk with pride — like Nebuchadnezzar — walk against God's righteousness; those who are saved from the fire "walk" as witnesses of divine power. Thus, our visible acts reflect our inner orientation.

sens: A person who crosses a territory, who moves from one place to another
H1982.detail: 1. The word simply designates a person in transit, who arrives in a place where they do not reside. In 2 Samuel 12:4, a traveler presents himself to a rich man: he is a stranger passing through, a guest who is not known and who asks for hospitality.
H1982.origine: This word comes from a Hebrew root (halak) that means "to go, to walk, to move." A traveler is literally someone who walks, who goes from one place to another. The same word can also designate the action of traversing a road or the movement itself.
H1982.emploi: The word appears twice in the Hebrew Bible. In 1 Samuel 14:26, in a context where honey is said to "flow" (the same Hebrew word is translated differently depending on the context: here it is the image of flow, of movement). In 2 Samuel 12:4, in the parable of the prophet Nathan, the traveler is a character who arrives at the rich man's house, and the latter refuses to touch his flock to receive him properly — instead, he steals the poor man's lamb. The word reinforces the idea of a foreign person, dependent on hospitality.
H1982.portee: This word reminds us that the Bible places great importance on welcoming the traveler and the stranger. Hospitality towards those who pass through is a moral duty: the rich man who refuses to properly receive the traveler using his own resources, and who steals from the poor instead, commits a grave injustice. This speaks to every believer about their responsibility towards those who cross their path.

sens: Tax levied on goods passing through a territory or road
Tax or fee that travelers or merchants must pay
General tax, tribute
H1983.detail:
1. The word primarily refers to a concrete tax imposed on goods in transit: in Ezra 4:13, the king decrees that Jerusalem will no longer pay this "right" of passage on goods crossing the territory. It is a tax on trade and movement.
2. More broadly, it is a fee that subjects must pay: in Ezra 4:20, powerful kings received "tribute, tax, and right of passage" from their peoples, three forms of taxation.
3. The term can also refer to any right or levy: in Ezra 7:24, the king exempts the priests, Levites, and temple servants from any "right of passage," meaning any tax or obligation.
H1983.origine: This Aramaic word comes from the Hebrew root הָלַךְ (halakh, "to walk, to go"). The initial image is that of passage, movement on a road: the right is what one must pay to pass. The Aramaic form reveals that this text from the Book of Ezra employs the administrative language of the Persian empire, very close to Hebrew but with its own nuances.
H1983.emploi: The word appears 3 times, exclusively in the Book of Ezra, in chapters 4 and 7, in the context of Persian royal taxation. In Ezra 4:13 and 4:20, it is associated with "tribute" and "tax" to depict the tax regime of the Persian kingdom: these are the three main types of levies. In Ezra 7:24, King Artaxerxes exempts the temple clergy, showing that this "right" was a general obligation. The context remains constant: the tax administration of the Persian empire and the privileges granted to the worship of the Lord in Jerusalem.
H1983.portee: This word reminds us that the Church and those who serve God enjoy special protections and privileges. The exemption from the "right of passage" is not due to civil power, but to the recognition of legitimate worship: it is a word of encouragement for the exiles who are rebuilding the temple. It also teaches that civil order depends on God and can be used to affirm religious freedom.

sens: Emit light, radiate
Glisten, shine brightly
Illuminate, light up a dark space
Manifest, appear with force (figuratively)
H1984A.detail:
1. Emit light, radiate: the word describes the physical action of a light source that produces and spreads light. In Job 29:3, God's lamp "shone" on the head of the righteous, an image of light that bursts forth and spreads.
2. Glisten, shine brightly: this means to shine with intensity and majesty, like the sun or the moon. In Job 31:26, the sun "shone" in its majestic splendor, showing the impressive radiance of a celestial body.
3. Illuminate, light up a dark space: to shine is also to dispel darkness and make visible. When the divine lamp "shone" in the darkness (Job 29:3), it guided the path of the righteous by dispersing the darkness.
4. Manifest, appear with force (figuratively): the word can evoke a brilliant manifestation, particularly that of divine favor or power. In Isaiah 13:10, the stars cease to "shine" during eschatological judgments, symbolizing the extinction of clarity and cosmic order.
H1984A.origine: The Hebrew word halal comes from a root that expresses the fundamental idea of shining and illuminating. It paints the image of light bursting forth, a luminosity that emerges and spreads. This root also evokes, in other forms, the idea of praising or glorifying — a rich connection: to praise is to make someone's glory shine. The word is used in the context of cosmic light (sun, moon, stars) and divine light (the lamp or favor of God).
H1984A.emploi: The word halal appears four times in the Hebrew Bible, exclusively in biblical poetry and wisdom (three uses in Job, one in prophetic Isaiah). It always describes a light that emanates, either from celestial bodies (sun, moon, stars) or from divine favor symbolized by a lamp. In Job 29:3, God's lamp shines as a sign of His goodwill towards the righteous. In Job 31:26, it is the sun and moon that shine in their natural majesty. In Job 41:9, even the monster Leviathan "shines" light through its sneezes — a hyperbolic image of its terrifying power. In Isaiah 13:10, this shining light goes out during apocalyptic judgment. The word always emphasizes the intense brightness and remarkable nature of luminosity.
H1984A.portee: For the believer, this word reminds us that divine light is real and active, guiding and directing those who receive it. It is not abstract or distant, but present and effective — it "guides in darkness." This word also invites us to recognize the splendor of creation (sun, moon, stars) as an expression of divine power. Finally, its use in apocalyptic passages underscores a serious truth: the light that God gives can also be withdrawn in judgment.

sens: Express admiration for someone, especially regarding their beauty or qualities
Speak well of someone by boasting about them to others
Honor God through songs, hymns, and joy
Recognize the greatness, power, and works of someone
Boast or take pride in oneself
Be worthy of praise, be famous
H1984B.detail:
1. Express admiration for someone: When Pharaoh's officers see Sarai's beauty, they "praise" her to their king, meaning they speak of her with admiration (Genesis 12:15). It is to recognize and communicate what is admirable about someone.

2. Speak well of someone, boast about them: When one "praises" someone to others, one recommends them, putting them forward by word. It is the act of saying good things about them, publicly celebrating them.

3. Sing the glory of God: The singers and musicians "led the songs of praise" (2 Chronicles 23:13). It is to express through music and song admiration and recognition towards God for who He is.

4. Recognize the greatness and works of someone: "Praise Him for His mighty acts!" (Psalms 150:2). To praise God is to proclaim and celebrate His powerful deeds and magnificence, inviting others to do the same.

5. Boast, take pride: The same root can mean to glorify oneself, to speak of one's own merits with vanity. It is to praise in one's own name rather than God's.

6. Be worthy of praise, have a good reputation: The name of the Lord must be "celebrated," meaning recognized as worthy of glory and honor from sunrise to sunset (Psalms 113:3).
H1984B.origine: This Hebrew verb comes from a root expressing the idea of shouting, proclaiming aloud. The word naturally evokes the action of making known, celebrating through word or song. The same family contains "Hallelujah," this cry of joy that literally means "praise Yah" (Yah being a shorthand for the divine name). It is a word very present in Israelite worship to express adoration.
H1984B.emploi: This verb appears more than a hundred times in the Hebrew Bible, mainly in the Psalms, Chronicles, and during the religious festivals of the people of Israel. The forms vary: one can be "boastful" about one's own merits, or one can "praise" God. In the Psalms, the verb is very frequent as a call to collective praise: "Praise the Lord!" (Psalms 146:10; 148:1-5). It is also used to express personal admiration or individual recognition (Psalms 69:31: "I will celebrate the name of God"). In the historical accounts of Chronicles, it describes the musicians and singers who offer praise during public worship celebrations. Its main meaning remains: to publicly and strongly express one's admiration or recognition.
H1984B.portee: This word invites the believer to come out of silence and express gratitude towards God, not through flattery but as a rightful reaction to His greatness and works. To praise God is to recognize that He is worthy of honor, which transforms our hearts by turning us away from ourselves. It is also a communal practice: the Psalms continually call us to "praise together," for praise strengthens the faith of the people. It is never a vain act, but the sincere expression of one who has recognized the power and goodness of God.

sens: A person lacking good sense, discernment, or wisdom
One who acts in a reckless or foolish manner
To behave like a fool, to act foolishly
To lose one's reason, one's judgment
To boast in a vain or unreasonable manner
H1984C.detail:
1. The fool is one who lacks wisdom and discernment: he does not understand the things of God and lives poorly (Psalms 5:6: "The fools shall not stand in your sight").
2. He is also one who acts in an unreasonable or excessive way, without restraint or caution. David, fleeing from King Saul, "pretended to be insane in their sight, and made marks on the doors of the gate" (1 Samuel 21:13): he feigned madness to escape danger.
3. The fool can also be one who boasts without foundation, who prides himself without reason — the psalmist says to the wicked: "Do not boast!" (Psalms 75:5).
4. The word finally describes one who has lost his judgment, his reason: God "makes the judges act foolishly" by rendering them incapable of discernment (Job 12:17).
H1984C.origine: The Hebrew root הָלַל (halal) fundamentally denotes the idea of shining, brilliance, or honor, but also that of acting foolishly or going astray. When vocalized הָלַל (halal in the sense of "fool"), it evokes one whose mind has strayed, who has lost his mental path. The same word, depending on the context, can mean to glorify (celebrate the brilliance) or to become mad (lose one's mind). It is a family of words that plays on the idea of what goes off its normal course.
H1984C.emploi: This word appears 9 times in the Hebrew Bible, mainly in the Psalms and wisdom literature, describing one who refuses divine wisdom. In 1 Samuel 21:13, David feigns madness before Achish to save his life. In the Psalms, fools are those who do not respect God and commit iniquity (Psalms 5:6), or who envy the happiness of the wicked due to lack of discernment (Psalms 73:3). The word also depicts one who boasts without reason (Psalms 75:5) or whose judgment is disturbed by God (Job 12:17, Isaiah 44:25). In the three usages in Jeremiah (Jeremiah 25:16, 50:38, 51:7), the context speaks of spiritual drunkenness, a madness provoked.
H1984C.portee: This word invites the reader to reflect on what constitutes true wisdom: that which recognizes God and obeys His word. The fool of the Bible is not primarily one who lacks natural intelligence, but one who refuses to fear God and seek His discernment. It is a call not to indulge in pride or boasting, but to ask God for the wisdom that gives meaning and stability to life.

sens: to brag arrogantly, to take glory in oneself
to exalt someone, to praise, to celebrate
to take pride, to put one's pride in someone or something
H1984H.detail:
1. To brag arrogantly, to take glory in oneself: it is to exalt one's own strength or exploits without real foundation. The king of Israel said to his adversary: "Let not the one who puts on his armor boast like the one who takes it off" (1 Kings 20:11), meaning: do not take glory in your war preparations before you have fought. Similarly, it is dangerous to boast of tomorrow: "Do not boast about tomorrow, for you do not know what a day may bring" (Proverbs 27:1).
2. To exalt someone, to praise, to celebrate: to praise God or someone else, to acknowledge their greatness. It is "to boast in God every day" (Psalms 44:9), that is, to recognize His power and kindness.
